item.content:encoded:
Well, that would have been fun.

According to ESPN’s NFL insiders Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport, the Denver Broncos have been checking in around the league for tight end help, and even checked in on Cardinals star tight end Trey McBride. The Cardinals made it clear to the Broncos that they have zero intention of trading the face of their franchise, and the Broncos have turned their attention elsewhere.

Schefter and Rapoport added that the Broncos have checked in around the league for tight ends, including Cardinals star tight end Trey McBride, who is from Fort Morgan, Colorado, and played at Colorado State. Unfortunately for the Broncos, the Cardinals made it known they have no intention of trading away the face of their franchise.

The Denver Broncos have checked in around the league on tight ends, going so far as to ambitiously — and some would say outrageously — check on Arizona Cardinals star Trey McBride, who is from Fort Morgan, Colorado, and played at Colorado State.

The Cardinals made it very clear they have zero intention of trading McBride, and Denver turned its attention elsewhere.

This has been a move many Broncos fans have been wanting them to make, and despite being in the basement of the NFC West once again, the Cardinals do not seem keen on the idea of trading away their star tight end. Still, it appears the Broncos are big fish hunting ahead of the trade deadline and would like to add a playmaker to their offense prior to the deadline this coming Tuesday.

As we know, they have been connected to Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor, but their level of interest seems to have lowered recently, with the New York Giants being the main interested team there. McBride would have been a huge and unexpected splash, so now we have to ask: what do GM George Paton and HC Sean Payton have cooking?

It’s clear they want to add a weapon to their offense and are willing to make a big splash if they can. The Colts are seeking a pricey package for Jonathan Taylor, and Trey McBride would have cost at least multiple 1st-round picks. So, what other running backs, tight ends, or, hell, even wide receivers are they looking to acquire?

One tight end to potentially keep an eye on is Eagles tight end Dallas Goedert. The pass-catching tight end market is not very good, but Goedert does seem like a player who could be available. With that said, he was a free agent this past offseason, and the Broncos did not show much interest at all; he ended up re-signing with the Eagles on a one-year deal.

A move at running back or tight end would make sense for the Broncos. The emergence of Jonah Coleman helps the Broncos’ backfield, but they still need more. Veteran JK Dobbins has really taken a step back this season and has struggled badly. Also, second-year back RJ Harvey and reserve/third down specialist Tyler Badie are currently on the IR. So, you could make a case that they need to add some depth to their running back room, even with Jonah Coleman playing well. As for tight end, they have veteran tight end Evan Engram who simply isn’t really used. He gets snaps but isn’t really targeted and feels like an afterthought in the offense. Adam Trautman is your blocking specialist and reserve/blocking tight end Nate Adkins leads the team in touchdown receptions (3), but only has 6 total receptions on the year.

The NFL trade deadline is Tuesday, November 10th at 2 p.m. MT, and our Denver Broncos appear to be a team that will be very active ahead of the Deadline.

item.content:encoded:
The NFL trade deadline is Tuesday, November 10th at 2 p.m. MT, and our Denver Broncos could be an active team prior to the deadline. They have been widely connected to Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor in the days leading up to the deadline, but according to 9NEWS Denver’s Mike Klis, the team could explore adding a weapon or two to their offense. He mentions running back, tight end, and wide receiver as the positions that they could add.

Looking at the Broncos’ needs heading into the deadline, the most glaring one is running back. Now, the emergence of rookie running back Jonah Coleman helps, but the Broncos still need more from the position. RJ Harvey and Tyler Badie are on the injured reserve, and veteran JK Dobbins has been struggling all season. So, adding another back to pair with Coleman would make sense.

The question is, will they go big and add a Jonathan Taylor or Breece Hall? Or make a smaller move for someone like Tony Pollard or someone else?

Klis mentions wide receiver, and while it may not be the most pressing need right now, it could be in a few months. Jaylen Waddle has not performed as expected thus far; Courtland Sutton will be 32 next season and has a large cap hit(Also restructured his deal and could be off the team next season); Pat Bryant has been very good, but has been on the IR; Marvin Mims is a pending free agent, while Troy Franklin is buried on the depth chart. Could the Broncos be looking to add a wide receiver who could contribute to this team this season and moving forward? This doesn’t seem as likely, but I wouldn’t rule it out if the right deal comes their way.

As for tight end, I don’t know. The only name that could move the needle and that might be available is Dallas Goedert, but is that even worth it? He would certainly improve that room, but the Broncos really do not utilize their tight ends in the passing game. Evan Engram has had a disappointing year, and blocking specialist Nate Adkins leads the group (and, funny enough, the team) in TD receptions with 3, but he only has 6 total catches thus far.

We’ll be tracking all the Broncos news and rumors throughout the weekend and right up to the deadline. It’s supposed to be an active deadline, so we’ll see if our Denver Broncos make any splashes or not in the coming days.

item.title: Saints Hall of Fame Honors Mark Ingram, Terron Armstead and Sal La Rock
item.description: Terron Armstead, Mark Ingram and Sal La Rock honored during annual Saints Hall of Fame luncheon
item.content:encoded:
On Friday, November 6, 2026, former New Orleans Saints left tackle Terron Armstead and running back Mark Ingram were inducted into the Saints Hall of Fame during a luncheon held at Chateau Country Club in Kenner.

Sal La Rock, the Superdome’s press box security supervisor, received the Joe Gemelli “Fleur de Lis” Award, which recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to the New Orleans Saints organization through their dedication, service and commitment to the franchise.

Ingram was selected by the New Orleans Saints in the first round (28th overall) of the 2011 NFL Draft. Over 10 seasons in New Orleans (2011–2018 and 2021–2022), Ingram cemented his place in franchise history, becoming the Saints’ all-time leading rusher in 2021. However, his record was surpassed by Alvin Kamara just three years later. A three-time Pro Bowl selection, including two appearances as a Saint, Ingram retired following the 2022 season and currently serves as a college football analyst for FOX Sports. Due to his commitments with FOX Sports, Ingram was unable to attend the luncheon but will be in attendance at tonight’s gala and tomorrow’s game. In a prerecorded message, Ingram expressed his gratitude to his family, former teammates, the Saints organization and the fans for their unwavering support, encouragement and love throughout his career, fittingly closing his message with an enthusiastic “WHO DAT!”

Armstead was selected by the Saints in the third round (75th overall) of the 2013 NFL Draft out of Arkansas-Pine Bluff. Over nine seasons in New Orleans (2013–2021), he established himself as one of the NFL’s premier offensive tackles and a cornerstone of the Saints’ offensive line. Armstead earned three consecutive Pro Bowl selections (2018–2020) and Associated Press second-team All-Pro honors in 2018. He played a key role in protecting quarterback Drew Brees and helping anchor one of the league’s most productive offenses during his tenure with the franchise.

During his acceptance speech, Armstead expressed his gratitude to his family, who were in attendance, as well as Saints owner Gayle Benson, who was also present, and the entire Saints organization for their support throughout his career. He also shared that his only regret from his playing days was that he and his teammates were unable to bring another Super Bowl championship to the city of New Orleans.

Sal La Rock has been a valued member of the Caesars Superdome staff since 1998, beginning his career in event services for public safety before being promoted to Press Box Supervisor just two years later. For nearly three decades, affectionately known as “Mr. Sal,” he has been a familiar face and a warm, welcoming presence for media members covering Saints games. His kindness, dedication and genuine hospitality have made him a beloved fixture in the press box, and game days at the Superdome simply wouldn’t be the same without him.

All three honorees will be recognized by the Saints Hall of Fame during halftime of tomorrow’s game against the Cleveland Browns.

item.title: NFL RB trade options include Jonathan Taylor – and possibly Breece Hall?
item.description: Jonathan Taylor is the best running back available on the trade market, but which other players could be dealt? Here are the top RB trade candidates.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 NFL trade deadline is rapidly approaching, and many contenders are looking to add talent to their rosters and gear up for potential Super Bowl 61 runs.

Already, NFL fans have seen a few major moves take place. The Indianapolis Colts offloaded a couple of their top veterans, left guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, while the Baltimore Ravens traded for Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett after Lamar Jackson suffered a significant thumb injury.

But still, there promises to be more trades before the deadline passes at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, Nov. 10; and some of the biggest potential chips that could move are at the running back position.

NFL TRADE DEADLINE CANDIDATES: Will the Jets spring another November surprise?

The prize jewel among potential deadline acquisitions is Jonathan Taylor, who the Colts are considering trading, but there are many other productive backs who could find themselves on the move before the deadline.

Here's a breakdown of the six best running backs who could be on the market ahead of the trade deadline.

NFL RB trade candidates 2026

Jonathan Taylor, Indianapolis Colts

If any big NFL fish is going to move ahead of the trade deadline, it will likely be Taylor. The Colts have signaled they are willing to trade the star running back amid their fire sale, and there are plenty of contenders that could use a dynamic, three-down running back to bolster their offenses for the stretch run.

Taylor has logged 812 scrimmage yards and eight touchdowns while serving as a catalyst for the struggling Colts. The second-round pick from the 2020 NFL Draft has posted at least 1,500 scrimmage yards three times in his career and twice led the NFL in total touchdowns and rushing attempts.

Taylor's workhorse capabilities between the tackles along with his strong pass-catching skills make him one of the league's best and most versatile running backs. The Colts are seeking a high price for Taylor, who is still just 27 and under contract through the 2028 NFL season, but teams like the Denver Broncos, Minnesota Vikings and Seattle Seahawks could all consider paying the price for the dual-threat star.

JONATHAN TAYLOR TRADE RUMORS: Ranking RB's best fits amid trade rumors swirl

Derrick Henry, Baltimore Ravens

The Ravens are a team that seems rudderless at the moment. They have lost four consecutive games to drop to 4-5 in the uber-competitive AFC North, and they also lost Jackson to a thumb injury that may prove to be season-ending.

Will the Ravens consider trading Henry with that in mind? Probably not, if their pre-deadline deal for Brissett is any indication. Baltimore may just try to stand pat and see if Brissett can provide steadier play at quarterback and lead the team to a playoff berth.

Still, the Ravens should probably consider dealing Henry, as Brissett has just a 23-50 record as a starter and has never made the playoffs. Henry remains one of the NFL's most bruising runners and is simply hard to tackle thanks to his 6-3, 252-pound frame and penchant for throwing powerful stiff-arms at his opponents.

Henry also has struggled without Jackson in the lineup, averaging 63 yards per game since Week 5, and is 32, which is long in the tooth for a running back. Henry will likely continue to buck the trend of decline for older running backs given his unique style, but if the Ravens can get commensurate value for the big-bodied back, it may behoove them to take advantage of that opportunity before he eventually does start to slow down.

Both the New England Patriots and New York Giants could use some depth at talent at running back, so reuniting Henry with Mike Vrabel or John Harbaugh could be an amicable solution for all parties.

RAVENS FUTURE: Should Ravens move on from Lamar Jackson after 2026? The case for and against it

Breece Hall, New York Jets

Trading Hall so soon after signing him to a three-year, $43.5 million extension may seem odd, but the emergence of Braelon Allen has given the Jets depth at the running back position.

Hall has missed the last five weeks of action, and during that time, Allen has averaged 100.8 rushing yards per game. Allen is still just 22 years old, so the Jets could decide to entrust him as their running back of the future as they continue to try to shape their roster into that of a playoff contender.

Such a decision would allow the Jets to dangle Hall and try to add to their already strong stash of draft capital, which includes three first-round picks in 2027. Hall is still just 25, so the explosive runner would likely draw a solid price on the open market.

The only question is whether Hall's quad injury would depress his trade value. If so, the Jets would probably be better served to hold onto him until the offseason, where they may be able to get better deals for him if he's fully healthy. His value could also rise if he can improve upon the paltry 3.2 yards per carry he has averaged early in the 2026 season, so holding him may be the most prudent move for the Jets.

Tony Pollard, Tennessee Titans

Pollard is a pending free agent playing for a Titans team that has posted a 1-6 record to open the 2026 NFL season. The 29-year-old doesn't fit the Titans' window for contention, so offloading him for a 2027 draft asset could help accelerate Tennessee's ongoing rebuild.

Pollard is on pace to log his fifth consecutive season with at least 1,000 rushing yards. He is a steady producer who is averaging 4.5 yards per carry this season and just had a two-game stretch during which he totaled 246 rushing yards and five touchdowns on 46 carries.

Pollard would be a great fit for any team that needs a running back but isn't able to land Taylor. The Broncos, Giants and Patriots stand out as the best potential options for the veteran.

Tyjae Spears, Tennessee Titans

Pollard isn't the only running back the Titans could consider trading. Spears never emerged as a lead-back for the Titans but he remains an explosive weapon and a quality receiver who can play the role of a third-down back for a contender.

Spears is set to be a free agent after the season and has missed time in recent weeks while battling a knee injury. As such, it wouldn't cost too much to land the 25-year-old, who could be revitalized by a change of scenery.

Vrabel coached Spears during his rookie year in 2023, when the Tulane product posted career-best marks in carries (100) and rushing yards (453). The Patriots could use some extra explosiveness and pass-catching depth at running back with TreVeyon Henderson battling a mysterious illness, so buying low on Spears could be a prudent move.

Kimani Vidal, Los Angeles Chargers

The Chargers' running game was supposed to be a three-headed monster in 2026 under Mike McDaniel. Instead, it has been a monster disappointment, with Omarion Hampton struggling badly and touches between him, Vidal and Keaton Mitchell varying widely from game to game.

Los Angeles may keep all three backs since they are relatively young, but the Chargers could also consider dangling one as trade bait to lower the number of cooks in the kitchen. Hampton was a first-round pick in 2025, so he won't likely be on the move, so that would leave Mitchell and Vidal as potential trade candidates.

While both would have appeal on the trade market, Vidal's tough-minded running style may make him the perfect player to dangle to teams needing a backup on the back-end of a strong one-two punch. The 5-8, 215-pound back is averaging 4.6 yards per carry this year and racked up 779 scrimmage yards and four touchdowns last year while starting in place of Hampton while the first-round pick was injured.

The Green Bay Packers could be a perfect spot for Vidal. They don't have much in the way of proven depth behind Josh Jacobs, and Vidal's presence would protect the team against any potential additional suspension Jacobs could face from his offseason arrest.

item.title: Saints vs. Browns: Key Matchups
item.description: The Saints are looking for a big win against the Browns.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints are attempting to get back in the win column and step up in a weak NFC South with a win over the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. But it won’t be easy. The Browns are 5-3 on the season and have found ways to win the tough ones. If New Orleans comes out with a win, it will be due to taking advantage of these key matchups.

Saints RBs vs. Browns run defense

The Saints are coming off one of the worst rushing performances of all time. They rushed the ball 17 times against the Pittsburgh Steelers for a total of 18 yards. In the loss, Saints running backs ran 14 times for 11 yards, averaging 0.8 yards per carry.

Fortunately for the Saints, they’ll be facing a Browns defense that has struggled against the run. Over the last two weeks, Cleveland is allowing an average of 170.5 rushing yards and three touchdowns per game. Although unlikely, reinforcements may be on the way for the Saints, with left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. returning to practice.

The run game is the biggest problem in New Orleans, and frankly, Kellen Moore’s career depends on correcting it. With a favorable matchup, the Saints should find success.

Saints pass rush vs. QB Shedeur Sanders

Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson has been placed in the concussion protocol and is unlikely to play. With it becoming more probable that second-year quarterback Shedeur Sanders will be starting, the Saints defense has a favorable matchup.

Chase Young has been dominant to start the season, and despite an early bye, he remains top three in sacks. Alongside Young is Carl Granderson, who has logged 5.5 sacks himself. The Saints have been one of the better pass-rushing teams in the league in terms of sacks, and their standout tandem is looking to have a big game against a young, inexperienced quarterback.

WR Jordyn Tyson vs. the Browns secondary

Sunday will be a big game for the Saints. They are returning from the bye to a home crowd, still within a game’s reach of the top of the NFC South. Despite all the implications, the biggest headline for New Orleans against the Browns will be the return of eighth-overall pick Jordyn Tyson.

Tyson will likely see his first NFL action on Sunday, and the Saints will be looking to get him started early. Tyson offers the catch-and-run ability the New Orleans offense has been missing, and he could be an immediate game changer. But if I know the Saints want to get Tyson the ball early, you could bet Cleveland knows it too.

Getting Tyson back is big for the Saints, and he could be the difference in a win or a loss, but the Browns will zone in on the momentum New Orleans will be looking to gain out of the bye, and it starts with the rookie.

item.title: Broncos vs. Panthers: 3 Players to Watch
item.description: In order for the Denver Broncos to defeat the Carolina Panthers on Sunday, these three players need to perform well.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos take on the Carolina Panthers on Sunday for their Week 9 matchup. If they can achieve a victory, they will be 7-2 before their bye week. In order to win and keep their spot atop the AFC West, the Broncos need these three players to play at a high level.

Nik Bonitto — Edge Rusher

Finding a way to rattle Bryce Young is one of my big keys to the game. So far this season, the Panthers’ offensive line has struggled to protect him. He has already been sacked 23 times—almost as many as last season—and he is getting pressured on over 40-percent of his drop backs.

Edge rusher Nik Bonitto is one of the players who needs to show up big on Sunday. After posting back-to-back seasons with double-digit sacks, the fifth-year pro is having a slower start to the 2026 season. Compared to 2025, Bonitto is experiencing a dropoff across the board relative to sacks, hurries, quarterback hits, and pressures.

Left tackle Rasheed Walker has been a liability for Carolina thus far. More often than not, Bonitto will be tasked with going up against him on Sunday. If he can have a big day and win his one-on-one opportunities versus Walker, that should definitely help slow down the Panthers’ offense which ranks Top 10 in many respects.

Malcolm Roach — Defensive Lineman

The Broncos boast a deep rotation along their defensive line. That has kept their line fresh and taken a big burden off of All-Pro Zach Allen’s shoulders. However, their depth will be tested on Sunday with Eyioma Uwazurike being ruled out. That means someone else is going to have to step up and be a dominant force in the trenches.

I’ve got a feeling Malcolm Roach will be that player. In eight games, the seventh-year pro has 24 tackles, 3.5 sacks, 5 tackles for loss, and 12 quarterback hits. Roach has always been a quality run defender, but his ascent as a pass rusher has been a great development for the team.

Being able to put pressure on Young (as mentioned above) will be critical. Though limiting running back Chuba Hubbard’s impact will be important too. Hubbard is on pace for a career season. He sports a great 4.6 yard per carry average and has 540 rushing yards with 5 rushing touchdowns on the season. Denver will need Roach to be quick off the snap and make some plays in Carolina’s backfield to slow him down.

J.K. Dobbins — Running Back

In a few articles this week, I’ve advocated for rookie running back Jonah Coleman to be the focal point of the Broncos’ rushing attack against the Panthers. Carolina’s defense has been awful stopping opposing rushing attacks in the first half of the season. That’s why it makes sense to pound the rock on the road.

Even if I’m bullish on Coleman deserving a majority of the reps, that doesn’t negate this being a big game for Dobbins. It absolutely is. He has struggled this season and is sporting a career low 3.3 yard per carry average. If he can’t find a way to improve going up against one of the NFL’s worst run defenses, when can we reasonably assume he will get on track? Denver needs a strong running game to be legitimate Super Bowl contenders.

Earlier in the week, Head Coach Sean Payton mentioned he was pleased with what he had seen from Dobbins thus far. However, rumors have swirled for weeks that the Broncos may be in the market to add to their stable of backs prior to the November 10th. How Denver’s run game looks, in particular Dobbins, against the Panthers might have an impact on whether or not they are buyers at the position before the deadline.

item.title: Miami Dolphins vs. Detroit Lions: Three Reasons Why
item.description: Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins will be back in Joe Robbie Hard Rock Stadium to face the Detroit Lions this Sunday.  The good news? For the first time all season, the Dolphins will not have to go back out onto the road after a home game.  The bad news?  They face a hot Detroit Lions team.  Do they have a chance?  Mebbe.

3 REASONS FOR HOPE

MALIK WILLIS IS IMPROVING

Locked On Dolphins covered an aspect of this much more deeply than I can in an article, so I’ll let you watch for yourself.  Willis was nothing short of atrocious the 1st 5 games.  He had moments but was overall bad.  But in the past 2 games, we have seen Willis take a step forward.  I’ve listed my preferred stats in previous posts so let’s compare Willis’ 1st 5 games to the last 2 games in those stats.  In the 1st five games, Willis had a completion percentage of 56.2% – completing 73 of his 130 attempts.  In the last 2 games, Willis has a completion percentage of 66% – completing 35 of 53 pass attempts.  In the 1st five games, Willis had a YPA of 6.53.  In the last 2 games, he has a YPA of 7.91.  He threw 2 TDs on 130 attempts for a TD% of 1.5%.  In the last 2 games, he has 4 TDs on 53 attempts, for a TD% of 7.5%.  Weeks 1-5, he had 4 INTs in 130 attempts for an INT% of 3.1%.  The last 2 weeks, he has 1 INT in 53 attempts, which is an INT% of 1.9%.  This is drastic improvement across the board.  Two games don’t erase the previous five and I’m not saying he has suddenly gone from Joe Dirt to Joe Montana.  But I said in the offseason he should be considered an “experienced rookie”.  And like most rookies, there has been bumps in the road but also some growth.  The next step is to maintain that growth and sustain these increased averages.  But not only is there statistical improvement, he has become a vocal leader.  Willis is a reserved man and doesn’t have a fiery disposition.  But his interaction with Ollie Gordon II on the sideline after Gordon’s penalty and what was said after that shows a level of leadership I haven’t seen from a Dolphins’ quarterback in YEARS.  It’s an impressive display for a young QB trying to find his footing and become a great player and a franchise QB.  They don’t HAVE to listen to him, but that interaction shows that they do.

THE REST OF THE OFFENSE IS GETTING BETTER

The Dolphins started the season very rough on the offensive side of the ball.  The were averaging 11.5 PPG the 1st 4 weeks of the season.  In the last 3 games, they average 23.7 PPG.  That would be 12th best if that were the season.  In the 1st 4 games, they average 267.5 yards per game.  In the last 3 games, they averaged 320 yards per game.  Getting Caleb Douglas back helped, but we’ve also seen development and improvement from other WRs like Malik Washington – who is creating more separation than I would have expected – and Kevin Coleman Jr., who roasted a Pats DB for his 2nd TD of the season.  Greg Dulcich is getting more involved.  Gordon had a rougher day at the office against a stout NE run defense, but he is still on pace for a 1000-yard season and maybe he gets double digit TDs.  It’s a young and growing offense that will have its fair share of issues, like we saw in the 3rd quarter last week.  But they are getting better and now face…

THE LIONS DEFENSE IS STRUGGLING

So far this season, the Dolphins have faced 4 of the top 10 scoring defenses.  They have faced 4 of the top 10 passing defenses in passing yards allowed.  They have faced 3 of the top 10 rushing defenses in yards per attempt allowed.  The Lions will not be any of those.  The Lions have the 31st ranked pass defense in yards allowed, with 1936, and 32nd in passing yards per game allowed at 276.6.  They are 26th in passer rating allowed at 101.0, 22nd in completion percentage allowed at 65.9, and 19th in YPA allowed at 7.3.  They are tied for last with 18 passing TDs allowed.  They have the 2nd highest ADOT for defender at 9.5, meaning teams are passing deeper on them.  They are solid tacklers, with the fewest missed tackles at 15 and are 5th in YAC allowed, but the Dolphins should have some success in the air against the Lions.  On the ground, the Lions are 6th in rushing yards allowed at 676 but also have the 3rd fewest attempts against them at 163. They allow 96.6 rushing yards per game and allowed 4.1 YPC.  As a scoring defense, the Lions rank just ahead of Miami (25.9 PPG), allowing 25.7 PPG.  Miami’s offense will have opportunities to move the ball and score.

3 REASONS FOR CONCERN

THE LIONS’ PASS RUSH IS STILL STRONG

Overall, the Lions’ defense looks like a weakness Miami could exploit.  But the Lions can get after the QB very well.  The Lions have 3 players with 4 or more sacks, led by standout edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson.  One of those players is IDL Alim McNeill and strong interior pass rushers have given Miami issues.  McNeill is ESPN’s top IDL pass rusher, with a win rate of 27%.  As a team, the Lions rank 3rd in PRWR at 59%. Perhaps Kadyn Proctor’s return can mitigate that problem, but after last week, I’m skeptical.  The Lions as a team are third in sacks with 24 and tied for 10th in pressure percentage at 24.8%.  The Lions don’t blitz at a high rate, ranking 17th at 25.7%, so most of those pressures are generated with a 4-man rush.  Miami’s OL will need to play much better than last week if they want to capitalize on the weaknesses of the Lions defense.

MIAMI’S PASS RUSH FACES A TOUGH TEST

The Dolphins’ defense has slowly started to move up the rankings of pressure percentage, currently 22nd at 21.1%.  They are still on the bottom of the barrel in terms of sacks, tied with KC and NYG with 9.  However, they have had at least 2 sacks in 3 of the past 4 games.  Chop Robinson has come on with 4 sacks and leads the league in pressure percentage individually and has the best pass rush win rate.  Unfortunately, the Lions have one of the best OLs in the league at stopping pressure. They rank 7th as a team in PBWR at 54% (see the previous link). PFF ranks them 1st and highlighted that the Lions’ OL only allowed 4 pressures last week to the league leading Vikings, who get a pressure 35% of the time.  Both of Detroit’s OTs are top 20 in PBWR (Paul has dropped out of the top 20).  The Dolphins and Jeff Hafley may need to get creative with pressure packages and blitz plans in order to get to Jared Goff.

THE LIONS ARE A VERY DANGEROUS OFFENSE

The Dolphins have faced some scary offenses this season, but none present the total package that Detroit presents.  The Chiefs have Mahomes and Walker, but don’t have elite receivers.  Cincy has Burrow and elite WRs, but their run game isn’t special.  The Lions have all of it.  They’re 4th in the league in total yards at 2768, but the 3 teams ahead of them have played an additional game.  They average 395.4 yards per game and 5.9 yards per play, tied for 5th.  They are 4th in passing yards per game at 264.0 and 7th in rushing yards per game at 131.4.  Goff is completing 67.7% of his passes, 5th best.  He’s thrown 15 TDs and only 1 INT.  Jahmyr Gibbs is 2nd in the league in attempts with 157, and 2nd in rushing yards with 773.  He has 8 rushing TDs, tied with several for 3rd, and leads the league in both yards per game at 110.4 and attempts per game at 22.4.  Gibbs also has 2 receiving TDs.  Amon-Ra St. Brown is 5th in the league in receptions with 53, 10th in yards with 571, and tied for 6th in TDs with 5.  One of those he is tied with is his teammate Jameson Williams. Williams doesn’t have the volume, with only 27 catches, but has 437 yards, meaning a 16.2 YPC average.  Of WRs with more than 20 catches, only Tee Higgins, Christian Watson, Rome Odunze, and Tre Tucker have a higher YPC average.  TE Sam LaPorta is tied with Williams and Gibbs in targets with 44 and has added 31 catches, 367 yards, and 3 TDs.  Those 4 players are Detroit’s primary weapons.  Only one other RB on the team – Sione Vaki – has any rushing attempts and all other pass catchers have 36 combined targets.  The Lions know who they are, what they have, and they lean heavily on it.  They are successful with it.  They are 3rd in scoring offense at 29.0 PPG.  The Dolphins’ defense?  Yeah, I’ve covered that.  They allow a ridiculous 76.9% completion percentage.  They have a good YPC average at 3.8 but have allowed 100+ rushing yards in the past 4 games.  Detroit is going to have their way on offense.  They can prevent a pass rush and can score in a variety of ways.  It is going to be ugly.

I SAID WHAT I SAID

This game could turn into a shootout.  Neither team is great defensively and both offenses have weapons they can use to exploit their opponent.  Miami is the less trustworthy of the two though and I would still expect the gameplan to be about running the ball, controlling the clock, and keeping the Lions offense on the sidelines.  Willis is improving though and this game has the potential to be more exciting, well, offense oriented than most would anticipate. As long as Miami can keep up. Too many fruitless drives could allow this game to get ugly very quickly. Can the Dolphins defense FINALLY plant a flag and get some stops?  Can the Dolphins offense and Willis carry some of this momentum into another week?

item.title: Report: Colts are in trade talks regarding QB Daniel Jones
item.description: The list of "multiple teams" currently includes the Ravens (who pivoted elsewhere) and the Vikings.
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis fire sale could indeed extend to the man who was supposed to become a franchise quarterback there.

According to ESPNFL, the Colts have engaged in trade talks this week regarding Daniel Jones, speaking to "multiple teams."

The precise language of the report identifies only one team as actually talking to the Colts. From the article, the Ravens "were one team to check in on Jones." The Ravens ultimately struck a deal with the Cardinals for quarterback Jacoby Brissett, whose plunge from No. 1 to No. 3 on the depth chart made it clear to the rest of the league that he was available.

The only other team mentioned by name is the Vikings, and the report points only to "[s]peculation" involving Minnesota. (We've been “speculating” about it since the immediate aftermath of Sunday's loss by the Vikings in Detroit.)

Past ESPNFL reporting on a potential trade for running back Jonathan Taylor ultimately listed five teams as talking to the Colts (Giants, Seahawks, Broncos, Packers, Vikings). The fact that other teams weren't mentioned as to Jones suggests that, frankly, there may not be other teams.

Really, which current contender would want him? The Vikings are the only potential playoff team that checks the box as possibly needing a starter right now. And only the Vikings and Giants are contenders with which Jones has direct experience. (The Giants wouldn't want a Jones reunion, and Jones surely wouldn't want it, either.)

That could change this weekend, obviously. One injury to a starter could alter the dynamics, spurring another contender to pick up the phone and make a push for Jones. The most memorable example of that came 15 years ago, when a broken collarbone to Raiders quarterback Jason Campbell prompted a quick deal for Bengals quarterback Carson Palmer, who had decided he didn't want to play for the team that had drafted him — and who had yet to report.

Three years ago, Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins popped an Achilles tendon two days before the deadline, forcing the Vikings to scramble at the deadline to do a deal with the Cardinals for quarterback Josh Dobbs.

Absent a multi-week injury to a starting quarterback on a contender that doesn't believe its backup can hold down the fort, the Vikings may be the only team that wants Jones at the deadline.

The preferences of Daniel Jones become a factor, too. If (as we firmly believe) he's not happy that the Colts folded the tents by trading guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner after a 2-5 start that included an overtime loss to the Chiefs and a toe-to-toe battle with the then-unbeaten Vikings, Jones would have a clear interest in hopping to a contender.

The Vikings wanted to keep Jones after the 2024 season. He opted to sign with the Colts in part because he saw a more realistic path to winning the job over 2023 first-rounder Anthony Richardson in Indianapolis than 2024 first-rounder J.J. McCarthy in Minneapolis. If he's told that a return to Minnesota would include being installed immediately as QB1, he'd surely prefer that to a lost season with the Colts.

Andd Jones has power over this process. Beyond the basic reality that no team wants a starting quarterback who doesn't want to play for it, the 2027 roster bonus and base salary that become fully guaranteed in March ($10.51 million) are currently guaranteed for injury. The ESPNFL article mentions that Jones could waive the injury guarantee in order to expedite a deal.

The reverse of that (Jones refusing to waive the injury guarantee) means that Jones could block a trade, if avoiding a potential eight-figure guarantee for 2027 is a dealbreaker for his prospective employer.

Our guess? Right now, only the Vikings currently have interest in Jones. And a trade for Jones becomes a very viable possibility if the Vikings lose to the Bills on Monday with Carson Wentz playing quarterback.

Given the possibility that another team will emerge as a competitor to get Jones, it's also possible that the Vikings have already decided to trade for Jones after Monday night's game — win or lose — and that the two teams have agreed to keep it under wraps until Week 9 ends.

Either way, if the oft-injured Jones plays on Sunday against the Cowboys and gets injured, that would kill any chance to trade him. That makes it important to monitor Sunday's game carefully. If the Colts apply a quick hook to Jones, it could mean that he's already gone.

item.title: Giants trade rumors: Ravens say Derrick Henry won’t be dealt
item.description: Also, updates on Jonathan Taylor, Vita Vea, more.
item.content:encoded:
Plan A for the New York Giants to upgrade at running back remains a mega-deal for Jonathan Taylor. Plan B, if there is a real Plan B, won’t be Derrick Henry of the Baltimore Ravens.

Per Adam Schefter, the Ravens have “informed Henry that they have no intention of trading him” to his former coach John Harbaugh and the Giants, or anywhere else.

The understandable logic behind that, from a Ravens point of view, is that the Ravens are not a) giving up on this season, or b) giving up on the idea that they can retain star quarterback Lamar Jackson long term.

Peter Schrager of ESPN added this on ‘GetUp’, per Pro Football and Sports Network:

“I don’t see it,” said Schrager. “My sense is this, talking to Baltimore’s sources: they have 12 draft picks in the upcoming draft, so draft capital doesn’t really do anything right now. They also play the Chargers, Panthers, Texans, Bucs the next four weeks. Those are winnable games. And they just traded for a quarterback; they traded for Cam Jurgens.”

“They’re not already in this selloff, fire sale mode. They are not Tennessee, they are not Indianapolis. That said, if there are calls about some other players they would probably be listening to some. I’m talking about guys who might’ve put themselves as veterans on the trade market themselves by the way that they’ve been performing in recent weeks.”

Justice Hill?

Schefter mentioned in his report that the Giants had asked the Ravens about the availability of veteran running back Justice Hill.

Hill was a 2019 fourth-round draft pick by the Ravens and has spent his entire career with Baltimore, so Harbaugh knows him well.

The confusing thing about interest in the 28-year-old Hill is that in seven seasons he has never carried the ball more than 84 times, and has just 301 carries for his career. There is nothing on his resume to suggest he is better than Tyrone Tracy or Devin Singletary. Unless the Giants are concerned about the hamstring injuries Tryone Tracy (currently on IR) and Cam Skattebo (doubtful vs. the Eagles) are dealing with and see Hill as an emergency fill-in, I’m not sure what he adds to the backfield.

Latest on Jonathan Taylor

The Athletic’s Jonathan Jones believes that the Giants and Minnesota Vikings are the favorites to convince the Indianapolis Colts to trade their star running back. Jones said he was told the Colts have already rejected an offer of a second- and fifth-round pick.

NFL.com also listed the Giants as one of the most likely landing spots for Taylor, and I believe the reasoning they offered is spot on:

A splash move at the deadline could go a long way to ensuring the Giants keep their division lead into January — and provide them a chance to pull off a postseason upset.

I believe that the Giants, with the investment they made in Harbaugh, would love to justify it with an NFC East title in Harbaugh’s first season. I also think they believe it would help set them up for the future, a future they believe Taylor can be part of for a couple of seasons.

In regards’ to Jones’ reporting that the Colts rejected a second- and fifth-round pick, what if the Giants made this offer:

A 2027 second-round pick, a 2028 fifth-round pick, and Tracy. If you are bringing in Taylor, and you have Skattebo, you don’t really have carries for Tracy. Why not include him in your offer in an effort to hold on to some of your draft capital?

Vita Vea too pricey?

We wrote Friday that Tampa Bay Buccaneers’ defensive tackle Vita Vea was reportedly on the Giants’ radar. Jones writes:

Vea signed a one-year, $30 million contract extension in August after protracted negotiations. It would be unusual for the team to deal him less than three months later, even if he has a low base salary in 2026 that can fit under anyone’s cap.

In the NFC South, furthermore, you’re always in it. The Bucs are a half-game behind Carolina for the division lead, and they hold the early tiebreakers over Carolina and Atlanta. A 3-5 record in Tampa looks radically different from a 3-5 record in Arizona.

I don’t think Tampa Bay would turn down a first-round pick for Vea, but I also don’t think any team is going to offer one for a 31-year-old with one season left on his deal.

Vea would help the Giants, but he also appears to be in decline:

Giving up a first-round pick would seem like a massive overpayment.

item.title: NFL news, live updates: Rams' Myles Garrett in line to return Sunday; Shedeur Sanders to start for Browns with Deshaun Watson in concussion protocol
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news ahead of Week 9.
item.content:encoded:
We're officially into Week 9 of the NFL season (and the looming NFL trade deadline), where teams will have to make a decision on the intended course of the remainder of their season — are they going all in? Or is it time to tear it all down and look toward the future?

NFL fans also await news on the fate of star running back Jonathan Taylor, who has been touted as a potential trade-deadline mover as the Indianapolis Colts kicked off their franchise reset with a fire sale. They've already traded away two foundational players, Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, for several draft picks as they look to the future, leaving us to wonder whether Taylor could be next.

The Los Angeles Rams could be a deadline buyer, as they've won back-to-back games and are already getting a long-awaited midseason reinforcement in the form of edge rusher Myles Garrett, a two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and the league's single-season sack record holder.

Garrett's in line for a return to game action on the road Sunday against the Washington Commanders. Coming back from early-season knee surgery that landed him on injured reserve, Garrett has practiced all week.

Shedeur Sanders will start at quarterback for the Cleveland Browns in Week 9 against the New Orleans Saints, head coach Todd Monken announced.

Deshaun Watson returned to practice in a limited capacity on Friday, but remains in concussion protocol. Monken said it's unclear if Watson will serve as the backup this week, though he will be listed as questionable

The Browns' No. 1 quarterback took a helmet-to-helmet hit during the first quarter of Sunday's loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers. Watson missed only four snaps, but later reported experiencing concussion symptoms on Monday night.

It is amazing how quickly the NFL season seems to go by, even more so with the Cleveland Browns actually winning football games before the NFL trade deadline. The Browns enter what seems like a must-win game in Week 9 versus the New Orleans Saints, with the result potentially impacting what GM Andrew Berry decides to do at the trade deadline.

Rumors have been strong around Cleveland looking at defensive end options. Recently, former Browns DE Jadeveon Clowney’s name hit the market, someone Berry tried to reacquire this offseason.

With Shedeur Sanders taking over for Deshaun Watson (concussion protocol) as the starting quarterback this week, a lot of the focus will, rightfully, be on the field in Louisiana, but the rumors around Tuesday’s deadline will continue to swirl as well. According to an Albert Breer rumor, the Browns are looking to be buyers and have two positions in mind:

The Browns are actually positioned now as buyers, which is pretty fascinating. Cleveland has looked around at adding a rotational edge rusher and perhaps a blocking tight end, which would free them up to move Harold Fannin Jr. around even more.

A tight end addition could have a bigger impact on the Browns offense than an edge rusher does on the defense. HC Todd Monken hasn’t used many extra offensive linemen in the blocking tight end role, leaving Fannin or receivers like Malachi Corley to step in there. Finding a quality blocking tight end could unleash Fannin even further while also helping their run game.

An edge rusher could make more direct statistical impact, and a defense can never have too many people to get after the passer.

item.title: 5 Things I Think I Think About the Miami Dolphins After Week 8
item.description: There’s still plenty to fix, but the future looks more interesting than the past.
item.content:encoded:
Let’s start with the bad news. The Miami Dolphins are 1-6, having scored the second-fewest points in the entire league. (Who’s scored the fewest? Thank you for asking. It’s the winless Los Angeles Chargers, whose offense is led by our old friend, Mike McDaniel. There’s a lesson in there somewhere.)

Young, developing teams can be hard to watch sometimes, but they can also be rewarding if you know what to look for. So with that in mind, here are five things I think I think after Week 8.

There’s a Good Team in There Somewhere

For one glorious half, the Dolphins looked like a quality, well-coached football team.

Their defense forced a fumble deep in Patriots territory. After trading field goals through most of the first half, they drove 70 yards for a touchdown, spreading the ball around to Greg Dulcich, Caleb Douglas and Kevin Coleman before connecting with Malik Washington for a short touchdown just before the break.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, things unraveled in the second half. The Patriots made adjustments the Dolphins couldn’t counter, and (as we’ll discuss shortly) Miami made so many self-inflicted mistakes that it couldn’t overcome them. But it’s hard not to wonder: If the Dolphins can build a double-digit lead over a playoff contender like the Patriots while making so many unforced errors, what happens when they stop making them?

That Said, the Dolphins Are Still Making Rookie Mistakes

Playing against a Mike Vrabel-led team isn’t going to be easy. Any lapses in communication on either side of the ball are going to be exploited, and the Dolphins weren’t exactly on their A game.

On one of Malik Willis’ five (!) sacks, Douglas and Bell ended up running to … the same area of the field. After stopping the Patriots’ offense to open the second half, the Dolphins had a chance to extend their lead. Instead, on third-and-9, Willis’ pass at the sticks doinked off Dulcich’s helmet. And at the end of the third quarter, two defenders covered the option on Drake Maye’s goal-line read-option, leaving Maye free to waltz untouched into the end zone. It didn’t cost them much, I suppose, but a wide-open Jaylen Wright also dropped an easy pass.

(And no, I’m not emotionally ready to talk about Ollie Gordon’s unsportsmanlike penalty.)

These are fixable mistakes, but they cost the Dolphins a winnable game against a division opponent.

Malik Willis Is Becoming Part of the Solution

OK, so 19 points doesn’t seem like much of an answer to the torches-and-pitchforks crowd around these parts three weeks ago. And even after two games of noticeable improvement, I don’t think we’re anywhere near being able to say, “Hey, let’s not spend an early-round 2027 pick on a quarterback.”

That said, 21-of-32 for 211 yards, two touchdowns and a deflected interception? That’s “pass”able (ha ha) for a quarterback playing with little help from the running game and under pressure for much of the afternoon.

More to the point, Willis is starting to do what professional quarterbacks do: throw the ball away, take the easy yards when they’re there and avoid putting the ball in harm’s way. (Though I see we’re still sliding behind the line of scrimmage for a sack instead of throwing the ball away, so there’s still some growth that needs to happen.) It’s a small thing, but a necessary one if you want to see continued development.

I’m eager to see how he performs against the Lions this week.

Kadyn Proctor’s Importance Is No Longer Theoretical

In my Tracking the Guards series, I’ve talked a lot about how people who understand offensive line play have been impressed with Proctor’s development this year, even if his PFF grades don’t always reflect it.

But if you really want to judge how well a player is performing, look at how the team does when he’s not in the lineup.

Proctor missed the Patriots game while in concussion protocol. His replacement, Jarrett Kingston, played fine, but Proctor’s absence was noticeable. Without him, the Dolphins’ running game lacked its power. There were far fewer instances of linebackers getting neutralized, and the Patriots’ safeties and second-level defenders had a much easier time disrupting the offense.

Proctor is expected back in the lineup against the Lions, and it’s clear the team needs him.

It’s Not Always Pretty, but the Rebuild Seems To Be Working

Just look at all the players 25 or younger who are either starting or playing meaningful snaps: Patrick Paul. Caleb Douglas. Malik Washington. Kevin Coleman. Chris Bell. Kadyn Proctor. Jacob Rodriguez. Michael Taaffe. Chris Johnson. Chop Robinson. Jordan Phillips. Jonah Savaiinaea.

You could probably throw in Kenny Grant, Dante Trader, Jason Marshall and Zeek Biggers, too.

That’s an incredible amount of development time, and it’s time that isn’t being spent (or wasted) on players like Jonnu Smith or Jalen Ramsey. And, with a few notable exceptions, they’ve largely stayed healthy, too. They’re getting the reps they need to grow into the players we want them to be.

Those reps are also producing penalties and blown assignments, but that’s part of the growth process, too.

So, yeah, 1-6 isn’t much fun, and it’s definitely not fun listening to pundits talk about how the Dolphins’ future opponents are going to have a field day playing them. But the growth and talent development are exciting to watch, and to me, much more rewarding than what we’ve seen in recent years: older players underperforming and getting hurt.

I like this version better.

item.title: 5 Bills to zero-in on at Vikings
item.description: How will Buffalo overcome the NFL’s No. 1 defense?
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills are off to a great start, sitting at 6-1 atop the entire AFC. The Minnesota Vikings are also off to a great start, and they are second in the NFC with a a6-1 record, as they are currently tired with the San Francisco 49ers.

The Vikings have the NFL’s best defense. The Bills have the NFL’s best offense. Something’s gotta give, as the move title suggests, and while I don’t expect to see Jack Nicholson in this one—or Diane Keaton, for that matter—I do expect to see a darn good football game.

If the Bills are going to come out on top, they’ll need all of their top players to perform to their capability. Here are five Bills to watch on Monday night.
_____________________________________________________________________________

QB Josh Allen

In a game like this, Allen has to avoid trying to do too much. Just take the checkdown. Take the easy money. Take the thing the defense gives you so that you can sustain the drive. Don’t come out juiced up trying to be a hero from the jump. Just play within the system, hit your keys, focus on your reads, and throw it to the guys wearing white helmets. If you do that, you’re probably going to leave Minnesota with a win. If you hold the ball, force it downfield into double coverage, and try to make chicken salad out of a far less desireable byproduct of chicken feed? Well, this is a defense that will make you pay. Allen doesn’t need to be Superman for the Bills to win on Monday. He just needs to be Josh Allen.

RB James Cook III

IF this stellar Vikings defense has a weakness, it’s the running game. They’re currently allowing opposing teams to average 4.5 yards per carry. That doesn’t bode well for the Vikings against the NFL’s third-best rushing offense. Cook averages 5.1 yards per carry this season, and Buffalo’s second-leading rusher—Allen—averages 4.9 yards per rush. If those two can take off, look out. The Bills worked Ray Davis into the rotation a bit more last week, which was nice to see. I’d like to see them do that a little bit more on Monday, as well, as Davis offers a different build and different running style to Cook. If Buffalo’s top back can find his footing, though, it will go a long way towards keeping the Bills on schedule, which will lead to points.

Injured Offensive Linemen

Which Buffalo offensive linemen will play? Alec Anderson missed Thursday’s practice with an ankle injury—is Austin Corbett going to slot in and start? Dion Dawkins missed practice with a rib injury—is Tylan Grable going to play left tackle just one week after starting in place of Spencer Brown at right tackle? Speaking of Brown, he was limited in practice thanks to his back injury. What happens if both he and Dawkins can’t suit up? Rookie Jude Bowry was terrible in the preseason, so making his first career start against the NFL’s top defense isn’t exactly ideal. The Bills could move Anderson out to tackle in pinch, but again, if he’s hurt too…what do the Bills do? The offensive line, and who is able to play, is a huge area of concern this week.

LB Terrel Bernard

Minnesota’s second most frequently targets receiver is tight end T.J. Hockenson. Bernard has been playing much better of late, as he seems to be settling in a touch in new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s scheme. The Vikings have struggled this year on offense, averaging just 20 points and 279 yards per game. However, Buffalo’s defense has also struggled, allowing 26 points and 352 yards per game. If Bernard can combine with Buffalo’s other linebackers and slot players to limit Hockenson, it will go a long way towards stymying a mid-level Minnesota offense. If he can’t, well, it could lead to a scenario where the moveable force (Buffalo’s defense) is pushed around by the immoveable object (Minnesota’s offense). Hopefully, Bernard continues his upward trajectory this week.

CB Christian Benford

Minnesota’s top receiving target needs no introduction, as Justin Jefferson is one of the NFL’s elite receivers. After a poor start to the season, Benford has thrived the last two games as an eraser for the opposing team’s top target. He traveled with Raiders’ tight end Brock Bowers and largely eliminated him from the game in Buffalo’s 33-30 victory three weeks ago. Then, last week, he traveled with Baltimore Ravens’ wideout Zay Flowers and completely erased him from the game, as Flowers logged the first zero-catch game of his career. Benford is a legitimate stud corner, and Jefferson is a legitimate stud wideout. This is a premier matchup, and I expect it to be one of the biggest keys to the entire game for both teams. If Benford can limit Jefferson, it will give the Bills a huge boost in the game.

item.title: Cowboys key matchup: Quinnen Williams vs the Colts interior OL
item.description: Quinnen Williams has the opportunity to take over the game against the Colts
item.content:encoded:
We have been saying the same thing for almost a month now, but the Dallas Cowboys are heading into a must win game in week nine with the Indianapolis Colts.

This is a unique matchup for the Cowboys due to the Colts practically punting on their season and moving on to 2027. In recent weeks, the Colts have traded away two of the best players on their roster in DeForest Buckner and Queneton Nelson, and their star running back Jonathan Taylor has dominated trade rumors over the last two weeks.

With the Colts not focusing on winning football games right now, and the Cowboys desperately needing a win, one of the biggest matchups in this game should be a massive mismatch favoring the Cowboys.

Early on in the season, it was fair to say Quinnen Williams was a bit disappointing. But over the last month or so, Williams has really turned it on and has been showing the dominant player we all expected to see in 2026. Since week five, Williams has recorded four sacks, three run stuffs, and 14 tackles. Williams has an intriguing matchup coming up in week nine against a depleted Colts offensive line.

The interior of the Colts offensive line took a big blow when Quenton Nelson was traded to the Seattle Seahawks. Taking his place at left guard was rookie fourth-round pick Jalen Farmer, who struggled mightily in his first start of the season in week eight. Farmer allowed three pressures, one hurry, and two QB hits against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

The Colts center has struggled this season too. Tanor Bortolini has allowed multiple pressures in every game this season except for two and has drawn six flags in the last four games. The Colts right guard, Matt Goncalves, has had a solid season so far for the Colts, but he is also a player Williams should be able to take advantage of as well in the running and passing game. Goncalves has allowed multiple pressures in the last two weeks.

This is an ideal matchup for Quinnen Williams who has been heating up here lately. Williams has registered 15 pressures and four sacks in the last three weeks, and this matchup should be one of the more favorable matchups he will see this season. Williams will need help from Kenny Clark and Otito Ogbonnia to keep some of the focus off of him, but this should be a matchup the Cowboys should win, and can be one of the biggest factors in them winning a much needed football game on Sunday.

item.title: Hear what Aaron Donald says about his botched fumble recovery in Week 8
item.description: Aaron Donald wants to recover fumbles and more NFL news on a Saturday
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Donald almost recovered a fumble in Week 8 against the Los Angeles Chargers, and had Donald actually recovered that ball, he may have scored a touchdown. Instead, Donald botched the recovery and he was left with nothing.

If you watch Donald talk about it, underneath the laugher for this blunder, he knows he needs to be better. He talks about the reality that if the Rams didn’t win, or if they were trailing, not recovering the ball wouldn’t have been such a laughing matter. Donald wants to be better for the Rams, and the Rams will need him and everyone to play at their best to recover from their 4-4 start.

Rams’ Aaron Donald Breaks Down Viral Muffed Fumble Opportunity (sports.yahoo)

“Donald explained that he may have gotten a bit too excited about the chances of scoring his first-ever defensive touchdown, which led to his missing out completely on the fumble recovery.

“Boom. I seen the ball. First thing came to my head. ‘Touchdown. I’m going to get this ball.’ I should have slowed down, but I felt people behind me like I want to get hit in my back. That’s going to hurt. So, I tried to go full speed and scoop it. The ball was going I thought the ball was going to bounce this way, but it bounced that way. And it just looked all damn silly,” Donald said.“

Aaron Donald gets brutally honest about Rams return (nypost)

“The 35-year-old three-time Defensive Player of the Year made a candid admission about his return to The Sporting Tribune’s Eric Lambkins II.

“No, it’s not what I expected, but we here,” Donald said of his return. He then added, “And I’m going to enjoy it though, you know. I’m enjoying the process. I’m enjoying myself week in and week out getting better. I’m enjoying being out there with the guys.”

“Ain’t what I expected, but I’m enjoying it,” he added.

Donald also spoke about getting Myles Garrett back healthy in Los Angeles’ upcoming game against the Washington Commanders, as Garrett has been sidelined since the Rams’ Week 1 game.“

Myles Garrett expected to play vs. Commanders (ramswire)

“The returns of Garrett and Ferguson will both be huge for the Rams, who have missed them over the last month-plus. Josaiah Stewart will now take on a more limited role in the pass-rush rotation, while Ferguson steps in immediately and becomes the Rams’ top pass-catching tight end.

With Davante Adams out, the Rams badly need another receiving threat, and Ferguson provides just that. Garrett, meanwhile, is the reigning Defensive Player of the Year and the record-holder for the most sacks in a season (23).“

NFL predictions: Washington Commanders vs Los Angeles Rams (sports.yahoo)

“Brown is a former playoff hero with the Commanders who lit up the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Detroit Lions during 2025’s playoff run, before wilting with 42 yards in the NFC Title Game against the Philadelphia Eagles. Burks has been ramping up his production this season with 12 catches for 233 yards and two touchdowns, including 81 yards against the Eagles on November 1. He is dealing with a left foot injury.“

Myles Garrett Set to Make Return vs. Commanders, But What Should Rams Expect? (si.com)

“The Rams traded for Garrett in what was their biggest acquisition of the offseason. However, shortly into training camp, Garrett began missing practices with what was described as knee soreness and then was placed on injured reserve that week as he underwent arthroscopic surgery. 

“There were just things I was dealing with mechanically that only continued to worsen as I played more throughout that game,” said Garrett on Friday. “It was rough and I was trying to avoid it, but you learn and you grow. Now it’s just a lesson that I had to learn from and I took the necessary steps to come back.”

With Jaylen Watson heading on injured reserve earlier this week, the Rams won’t get a look at what their defense could have been with Garrett, Watson, Trent McDuffie, and Aaron Donald. However, the Rams will get a look at what their defense can do with Donald and Garrett on the field together for the first time.“

Myles Garrett’s Expected Return Gives Los Angeles Rams a Pass-Rush Boost (athlonsports)

“Locked On Rams Squad Show host Gavin Carlson said Garrett can help compensate for Watson’s absence by shortening the time Daniels has to diagnose coverage. Carlson’s central point was not that one pass rusher erases the loss of a productive cornerback; it is that Garrett can force quicker decisions, creating more manageable coverage situations for the defensive backs who remain.”

Rams safety Quentin Lake apologizes to Justin Herbert for ‘deli meat’ comment, even though he has a point (sports.yahoo)

“According to The Los Angeles Times, Lake sent an apology to Herbert over text message, but had not heard back.

“I don’t know if he read it,” Lake said. “He probably says, ‘I don’t care about it anymore. I’m not trying to see this. It doesn’t matter. You said what you said.’ But at the same time I … felt like it was right for me to at least say, ‘Hey, man, I didn’t mean it in any disrespectful way.'”

Come on, Justin: He meant you were throwing deli meat in the most respectful way imaginable!“

Rams listed Matthew Stafford with elbow injury because reporters asked about ice on it (sports.yahoo)

“Really, it’s because you guys asked me about it earlier in the week,” McVay told reporters on Friday regarding the decision to disclose an elbow injury for Stafford. “It’s more semantical than anything else. It’s normal, like what he told you guys, but because you guys asked me about him having ice on his elbow. . . . He’s been full, hasn’t missed any sort of reps so normal management stuff that he’s been doing over the last few years.”

It conjures memories of the Patriots’ one-time habit of listing former quarterback Tom Brady as “probable” with a “right shoulder” injury. That all started because he had ice on his shoulder in the locker room, reporters inquired, and the team decided to just put him on the injury report every week.“

“Grant Stuard will be limited with his hamstring. He’ll be questionable for the game. Jordan Whittington will be limited with his back. He’ll be questionable for the game. Rams & Commanders set for a crucial NFC showdown in Week 9 | Game Preview (therams.com)

“Key contributors continue to peel off to the injured list, sapping what should be some nice momentum for the Rams.

When you think back to how this roster was constructed, it’s deflating to come to grips with the fact that we’ll see zero snaps of Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, Myles Garrett, and Aaron Donald playing football together in 2026.

“I think you’ll miss the production, the toughness, some of the different things that we’re able to do with him,” Sean McVay remarked this week as Watson accepted season-ending surgery on his twice-injured shoulder. “A couple of weeks ago, he’s cramping at the Raiders game and he says when he’s getting an IV, ‘Give me half a bag. I need to get back out there.’ He’s been awesome. He’s been playing through some different stuff, but he’s been really productive, and it’s unfortunate that that happened.”

item.title: Detroit Lions vs. Miami Dolphins preview: 3 key stats
item.description: A data-driven preview of Lions at Dolphins, focusing on key stats and matchups.
item.content:encoded:
As the Detroit Lions approach the midway point of their season, it’s been a weird and challenging week to care as deeply about football or celebrate the Vikings win. Most Lions fans, media members, and those within the franchise have been clinging to the progress reports and updates on team captain Jack Campbell, who remains hospitalized with a neck injury suffered in Week 8. The player who was awarded last season’s media Good Guy of the Year award had just welcomed his first child with his wife, Megan, a son named Cooper, in July. And here was the new dad laid up in a hospital bed, still without full movement of his upper body. It was tough to harness that same giddy, football-frenzied feeling for the upcoming game until fans were reminded why this is such a likable team, as Campbell, the player who perfectly embodies this city and this franchise, remained at the forefront of players’ and coaches’ minds throughout the week. They spoke about how they’re playing for 46.

Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard said, “Let’s play and prepare like 46. The way you honor him is to wipe those tears from your eyes and make sure you prepare and play like him.”

That’ll get you on board to root for the boys quickly. And suddenly, just like the countless games down the stretch in 2024 that were continually billed as “trap games,” you feel reassured that the Lions won’t let the 1-6 Miami Dolphins sneak up on them. They’ll be looking to fight and take care of business against the team that once called Dan Campbell its head coach and had Sheppard as one of its defensive anchors.

The Dolphins are going through a rebuilding period, but head coach Jeff Hafley and general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan both come from Green Bay and are all too familiar with the Lions. They have their talent-deficient unit losing but competing, with a number of young players who could become foundational pieces, much like the early Dan Campbell Lions. This week’s preview will examine three key stats and matchups Detroit needs to control to keep its three-game winning streak alive, avoid giving the Dolphins life, and make 46 proud.

Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus.

Good Golly, Miss Ollie

This week’s preview will focus entirely on how the Lions’ defense will coalesce to cover for the absence of Jack Campbell, and how the Dolphins’ offense will understandably try to attack a defense without its green dot. Linebackers Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske are expected to handle the primary linebacker snaps, all with expanded roles and added responsibilities. That becomes particularly important given Miami’s recent success pounding the rock with Ollie Gordon since the De’Von Achane injury.

The Dolphins comparisons to the early Dan Campbell-era Lions have been prevalent this week, and one reason for that is Miami’s reliable and developing offensive line. From left to right, Patrick Paul, Kadyn Proctor, Aaron Brewer, Jonah Savaiinaea, and Austin Jackson form an above-average unit with a good mix of proven, reliable veterans and young, ascending players. They’ve started to give the Dolphins a fighting chance by being imposing and winning at the line of scrimmage.

Since Week 4, the Dolphins have shifted their rushing approach, leaning into their offensive line and Gordon’s preferred running schemes by utilizing power concepts on 13.8% of runs (5th) and man/duo concepts on 20.7% of rushing attempts (15th), with considerable success.

With power, which features a backside pulling guard attacking the frontside like a runaway freight train, Miami has averaged 5.7 yards per carry (7th), +0.219 EPA/rush (6th), a 56.3% rushing success rate (5th), and a 25.0% explosive run rate (4th) since Week 4. Power runs will require Detroit’s linebackers to not only process and flow quickly, but also meet the pulling guard in the hole without giving up ground and scrape from the backside. The linebackers need to be firing on all cylinders to match Miami’s physical, downhill approach.

The same goes for defending man/duo concepts, where the Dolphins’ offense has churned out 5.1 yards per carry (5th), +0.122 EPA/rush (5th), a 50.0% rushing success rate (5th), and an 8.3% explosive run rate (15th) since Week 4.

Interestingly, teams haven’t really tested the Lions’ defense with power runs this season, with only 3.1% of rushing attempts (31st) coming on power concepts. Detroit has faced just one such rush since Week 4, which went for minus-4 yards. The Lions have fared well in the small sample size, allowing only 3.4 yards per carry (t-11th) and no explosive plays on their limited snaps defending power. Teams have, however, tested the Lions’ defense up the gut with man/duo concepts, running them on 31.3% of rushing attempts (5th). Detroit has countered that volume by cleaning up those physical runs, allowing just a 33.3% rushing success rate (4th) and 0.6 yards after contact per rush (2nd).

An underrated key to preventing the Dolphins from outmuscling Detroit up the middle with power and man/duo concepts will be whether Tyleik Williams can play with his hair on fire against All-Pro center Aaron Brewer. Brewer understands leverage and angles better than most centers in the league, but he’s also a pivot player who stands just 6-foot-1 and 290 pounds. If the 6-foot-3 Williams, who notably lost a ton of weight this spring to get down to just 325 pounds, can win at the point of attack, overpower Brewer into the backfield, disrupt rushing lanes and timing, and congest the flow of the run play, it’ll go a long way toward making the linebackers’ jobs much easier.

God Forbid a Willis Gets a Little Motion

While the Dolphins’ offense under second-year holdover offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik, formerly of the Houston Texans, doesn’t do much well outside of some aspects of its run designs, it does one thing often enough that it might challenge the Detroit Lions’ defense.

The Dolphins’ offense uses pre-snap motion on 74.1% of its snaps, the second-highest rate of any team in the NFL. The league average is only 59.2%, while the Lions’ offense, for comparison’s sake, sits at just 54.5% (24th). What’s interesting is that the Dolphins aren’t particularly better at rushing or passing the football with or without pre-snap motion, remaining bottom 10 in most metrics. The prevalence of the pre-snap motion itself is what’s important here.

The Lions’ defense hasn’t been tested as frequently against pre-snap motion this season, and when it has, there have been some struggles. Detroit has faced pre-snap motion on only 52.1% of its defensive snaps, the second-lowest rate in the NFL.

The Lions have actually excelled at defending the run against pre-snap motion, restricting opponents to -0.16 EPA/rush (4th) and just a 36.7% rushing success rate (4th). Detroit has managed to shut down offenses trying to gain an advantage in the numbers game, manipulate gap assignments, or use motion to stretch the defense geometrically, get defenders out of position, and create rushing lanes. However, issues arise in pass defense against pre-snap motion. Even if the Dolphins haven’t been particularly successful using it, there are still some concerns for Detroit.

Opponents have passed on 63.6% of plays featuring pre-snap motion against the Lions’ defense, the highest pass-to-run ratio in the NFL on such plays. Against pre-snap motion, Detroit’s pass defense has allowed +0.22 EPA/dropback (29th), a 54.1% passing success rate (26th), and an 11.6% explosive pass rate (27th).

The Lions’ coverage unit will need to communicate effectively and trust one another, particularly with a new green dot in either Derrick Barnes or Malcolm Rodriguez and defensive backs adjusting their coverage responsibilities based on the motion. They’ll need to keep an underrated Dolphins receiving group featuring the springy Malik Washington, promising rookies Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell, and Kevin Coleman, and tight end Greg Dulcich from getting loose and allowing Malik Willis to chunk the ball downfield.

Where There’s a Willis, There’s a Way

Since Week 5, Kelvin Sheppard and the Detroit Lions’ defense have blitzed on only 17.3% of dropbacks, the second-lowest rate in the NFL (the Dolphins, interestingly, are the lowest at 16.1%). In that same span, comparatively, the Vikings have blitzed 75.6% of the time. It’s a noticeable difference for the Lions’ defense over the last month, considering that in Weeks 1-4, Detroit was tied with Miami at a 27.4% blitz rate (t-17th). Sheppard has dialed back the aggression, allowing more defenders to remain in coverage and letting the front four go to work.

That approach remains the best fit for this matchup, as Malik Willis, just like lawyer Walt Worsch with dog bites in Detroiters, is a bit of a mack when it comes to facing extra pass rushers.

Against the blitz, Willis has a 3:0 touchdown-to-interception ratio, a 94.8 passer rating (18th out of 35 qualifying quarterbacks), 6.6 yards per attempt (22nd), and a 46.7% passing success rate (21st). While those numbers aren’t particularly impressive, they’re surprisingly better than his numbers when he doesn’t face a blitz. There’s a reason teams are blitzing the Dolphins on only 30.4% of dropbacks (18th).

As a team, the Dolphins are also averaging 7.1 yards after catch per reception against the blitz, the third-highest mark in the NFL behind only the Bills and Chiefs. Malik Washington is by far Willis’ favorite safety valve when opposing defenses bring extra heat. This season against the blitz, Washington has recorded 16 targets, 14 receptions, 177 receiving yards, one receiving touchdown, and +10.4 receiving EPA (11th). Washington’s 87.5% catch rate on blitz targets ranks tied for fourth among all wide receivers.

Kelvin Sheppard will need to have the patience to let his four-man pass rush get home against Willis. That also means having linebackers Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske spend less time firing at the quarterback and more time in coverage. Without their captain directing traffic, how Sheppard balances those coverage responsibilities and keeps Willis from exploiting the blitz will go a long way toward determining whether Detroit can make it four straight wins.

The nation’s capitol eleven currently stands at 2-4-1 and are coming off a 27-10 win over the Philadelphia Eagles.

Washington’s offense is ranked in the bottom third of NFL teams for the season, but have trended upward slightly over the last three games with the return from injury of quarterback Jayden Daniels. The Rams have had their struggles defending athletic quarterbacks who can extend drives with their running ability and Daniels is adept at that. While injuries have detoured his and the team’s success since his Rookie of the Year performance in 2024, he is still dangerous and has yet to throw an interception in 2026.

Daniels does good work spreading out the receiving targets, veteran Stefon Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams being the primaries.
