item.title: Future Broncos: 3 Prospects to Watch in Week 10 of NCAA Football Season
item.description: Here are three draft prospects Broncos Country should keep their eyes on in Week 10 of the collegiate football season.
item.content:encoded:
Week 10 of the NCAA Football season is upon us. After a multi-week hiatus from talking prospects to give my thoughts on the NFL trade deadline and last week’s mock draft—it’s back to the grind to highlight some options for the Denver Broncos in the 2027 NFL Draft. For this installment, I decided to make it focused on defense.

Jaylen McClain — Safety — Ohio State

The Broncos have gone through a lot of injuries in their secondary this season. Multiple starters at cornerback and safety have missed a few games. They’ve had to really embrace the next man up mentality in their defensive backfield.

Even so, they have performed well as a unit. However, the future of the group is uncertain with a handful of players scheduled to be free agents at the end of the season. We all know General Manager George Paton loves drafting defensive backs. With nine picks in this year’s draft, I have no doubt at least one of them will go to the backend of the Broncos’ defense.

Just to be clear, I’m not advocating for drafting a safety with a premium selection. However, Future Broncos serves as an exercise to highlight good prospects that fit the team at any position of need. One player that is flying up draft boards is Ohio State safety Jaylen McClain.

As a freshman, McClain (6’0”, 203 pounds) appeared in fifteen games for the National Champion Buckeyes and posted 15 tackles. Last season as a sophomore, he earned a starting role in their secondary. He didn’t disappoint and notched 53 tackles and allowed just a 67-percent passer rating when targeted.

This season, he has improved even more. Through eight games, the junior safety has posted 37 tackles, 1 sack, two interceptions, and a forced fumble. The big play aspect of the game [forcing turnovers] that was missing earlier in his career finally has started to show out.

Ohio State Defensive Coordinator Matt Patricia deploys McClain in a variety of fashions. He has the athleticism and talent to be a true centerfield type safety in the NFL. He doesn’t just excel in coverage; McClain is aggressive against the run and has been disruptive when used on blitzes.

Does that sound like a player that would fit Denver’s’ defense? Absolutely. Though I question whether or not Denver would make the premium investment it would take to select him if he declares. He seems like a sure-fire Top 50 pick. You can catch McClain in action when the #11 ranked Buckeyes host Oregon this afternoon.

Sebastian Cheeks — Edge Rusher — Wisconsin

Prospect development certainly isn’t linear. Sometimes it takes a few seasons for players to hit their stride to showcase their potential to play at the next level. Wisconsin fifth-year senior edge rusher Sebastian Cheeks is one of those players.

Cheeks (6’3”, 243 pounds) spent his first two years at North Carolina where his impact was limited to just 11 games due to a shoulder injury. In 2024, he transferred to the Badgers in order to get more playing time and try to revitalize his collegiate career. He played in 23 games in his first two seasons with Wisconsin but was still mostly a backup.

This season, Cheeks has been dominant after earning a starting role. In fact, he is looking like one of the best pass rushers in the entire nation. In eight games, Cheeks has notched 31 tackles, 8 tackles for loss, 6 sacks, and two forced fumbles. He is currently posting an impressive 23.9% pressure rate—the best of any draft eligible defender in this class.

My biggest question mark with him is how well he set the edge as a run defender in the pros at his size. It’s not necessarily a liability now, but it may be going up against NFL talent every Sunday. While I do think the Broncos have much larger and immediate needs than edge rusher, but you can never have enough pass rushers. If Cheeks keeps dominating, he will easily be a Day 2 pick half a year down the road. You can catch Cheeks in action this afternoon when the Badgers host Rutgers.

A.J. Holmes Jr. — Defensive Lineman — Texas Tech

The Broncos certainly have one of the deepest defensive lines in the National Football League. Whether or not Denver opts to invest significant draft capital next Spring remains to be seen. They have utilized third-round picks the past two drafts to bolster the unit’s long-term potential.

However, Eyioma Uwazurike is a free agent and D.J. Jones carries a hefty cap hit for a player that sees only 40-percent of the defensive snaps. Winning in the trenches is a formula for success. I’m a strong advocate of always adding firepower to the offensive and defensive lines. A prospect that has made a monumental impact this collegie season is Texas Tech defensive lineman A.J. Holmes Jr.

Holmes Jr. (6’3”, 300 pounds) spent his first three seasons at Houston. A reserve and depth player for his first two years, he was 12-game starter for them in 2024 and posted 40 tackles, 8.5 tackles for loss, and 2 sacks. In 2025, he transferred to Texas Tech for more exposure and to get on the radar of NFL scouts and general managers.

He started the season as a backup for Joey McGuire’s squad but finished out the last eight games of the year as a starter in the Red Raiders’ defense. He had a quality season and posted 38 tackles, 9 tackles for loss, 4.5 sacks, with 2 fumble recoveries, and 1 forced fumble.

This season, Holmes is playing the best ball of his life with the Red Raiders. At the midway point of the season, he already has 25 tackles, 7.5 tackles for loss, and 7.5 sacks and 1 forced fumble. He leads all interior defensive lineman in the nation with a whopping 33 quarterback pressures.

His physical traits may not be elite. Though he makes up for them with an incredible motor, feisty demeanor on the field, and having a wide variety of pass rushing moves. He lines up all over their defensive front and is just as disruptive going up against tackles as he is interior offensive linemen.

If Holmes Jr. continues to play this great, he will certainly be an All-American and a good bet to be selected in the Top 50 picks in the 2027 NFL Draft. You can catch Holmes in action tonight when the 13th ranked Red Raiders host West Virginia.

item.title: Chicago Bears Week 9 Flashbacks: A Pair of Wins Against Rivals and a Defensive Masterclass
item.description: Hop aboard the Gridiron Time Machine with @iamcogs and take a trip down Week 9 Bears memory lane!
item.content:encoded:
Climb aboard the Gridiron Time Machine as we revisit three memorable Week 9 performances from Chicago Bears history!

1.) 1990, Bears @ Buccaneers: Testaverde throws it to everybody

November 4, 1990 | Bears win 26-6

The Bears entered Week 9 of the 1990 season at 7-1 and firmly in control of the NFC Central.

Tampa Bay quarterback Vinny Testaverde probably wishes this particular Sunday had gone a little differently.

After a scoreless opening quarter, Chicago finally broke through with a 12-yard touchdown run from Brad Muster. Neal Anderson added another score later in the quarter, while Kevin Butler’s 30-yard field goal sent the Bears into halftime with a 17-0 advantage.

The offense did its part, but the defense completely took over the afternoon.

Testaverde completed just 10-of-24 passes for 149 yards while throwing five interceptions and losing a fumble. Rookie safety Mark Carrier grabbed two of those interceptions within a two-minute span late in the second quarter, helping set up 10 Chicago points. Richard Dent, Shaun Gayle and Ron Rivera each added interceptions of their own.

Jim Harbaugh quietly put together a solid afternoon on the other side, completing 14-of-23 passes for 213 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions. His 19-yard scoring strike to Dennis Gentry helped extend the lead to 23-0 in the third quarter.

Chicago piled up 378 yards of offense, including 187 on the ground, while controlling the football for more than 38 minutes. Tampa Bay did not finally reach the end zone until the fourth quarter, long after the game had been decided.

The Bears walked out of Tampa with a 26-6 victory and an 8-1 record.

Five interceptions, six total takeaways and another dominant performance from a defense loaded with familiar names.

That sounds like a pretty good Sunday against Tampa Bay.

2.) 2013, Bears @ Packers: McCown gets it done at Lambeau

November 4, 2013 | Bears win 27-20

Walking into Lambeau Field without your starting quarterback is generally not an ideal recipe for success.

The Bears found a way anyway.

With Jay Cutler sidelined, veteran backup Josh McCown made his first start since the end of the 2011 season against a Packers team sitting atop the NFC North.

The complexion of the game changed almost immediately when Shea McClellin sacked Aaron Rodgers on Green Bay’s opening possession. Rodgers suffered a fractured left collarbone on the play and did not return, leaving Seneca Wallace to finish the game.

That turned Monday Night Football into a battle of backup quarterbacks, and McCown was more than ready for it.

He completed 22-of-41 passes for 272 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Brandon Marshall caught seven passes for 107 yards and a score, while Matt Forte rushed for 125 yards and another touchdown.

Green Bay managed to turn a 17-10 halftime deficit into a 20-17 lead in the third quarter without Chicago’s offense touching the football, scoring a touchdown before recovering a surprise onside kick.

McCown answered.

He found Alshon Jeffery for a six-yard touchdown late in the third quarter to put Chicago back in front 24-20. From there, the Bears put together a clock-killing fourth-quarter drive that eventually ended with a Robbie Gould field goal and a 27-20 victory.

McClellin finished with three sacks, matching his career total entering the night, while Chicago’s defensive ends combined for five sacks overall.

The win snapped Green Bay’s six-game winning streak against the Bears and created a three-way tie atop the NFC North at 5-3.

A backup quarterback, Lambeau Field and Monday Night Football.

Not a bad time for one of the best performances of McCown’s Bears career.

3.) 2018, Bears @ Bills: The defense does the scoring

November 4, 2018 | Bears win 41-9

The 2018 Bears were beginning to figure out just how dangerous their defense could be when they traveled to Buffalo in Week 9.

The Bills got the full experience.

Chicago’s offense managed just 190 total yards, Mitchell Trubisky threw for only 135 yards, and the Bears possessed the football for less than 26 minutes.

Naturally, they scored 41 points.

After a scoreless first quarter, Jordan Howard punched in a one-yard touchdown to give Chicago the lead. Then the defense decided to handle the scoring itself.

Eddie Jackson stripped tight end Jason Croom, recovered the football and raced 65 yards for a touchdown. On Buffalo’s next possession, Kyle Fuller broke up a pass that Adrian Amos intercepted.

Watch the full game below:

One possession later, Fuller did it again.

This time the deflection landed in the hands of Leonard Floyd, who returned the interception 19 yards for another touchdown.

Chicago had forced turnovers on three straight Buffalo possessions, scored twice on defense and suddenly held a 21-0 lead. Howard added another touchdown before halftime to make it 28-0.

The Bears defense finished with four takeaways, three interceptions and four sacks. Jackson and Floyd accounted for 14 points by themselves, while the Bills offense scored just nine.

Chicago cruised to a 41-9 victory, improving to 5-3 and maintaining its lead in the NFC North.

There may not be a stat that sums up the 2018 Bears better than this one:

41 points. Just 190 yards of offense.

Sometimes the easiest way to fix an offense is to let the defense score instead.

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Big Blue View mailbag: Trade deadline, McCarthy vs. Dart, more questions
item.description: The mail’s here! Questions and answers about the Giants.
item.content:encoded:
Isaac L. Scharf asks: Hello, do you really believe that the Giants are contenders, or are they pretenders? We may be seeing a little bit of last year’s Patriots given the fact that we haven’t played a single team over .500. So do you think the Giants are contenders or pretenders?

Ed says: Isaac, the standings say they are contenders. The oddsmakers say they are the favorites to win the NFC East. The way everyone else in the division has played absolutely tells us that the Giants should be in the race for the division down to the wire.

Pretenders? Well, yes, if you think of them as a team that will or should be a legitimate Super Bowl contender.

I say just take the ride, enjoy it, and don’t try to label the Giants as anything.

Chris Holland asks: I am wondering if the NFL has made any statements regarding the rampant use of the “peanut punch”. From a safety perspective this is an accident waiting to happen. Ball carriers are going to start suffering injuries to their hands and lower arm as the result of having very large and strong defenders throw full force punches at the ball. I have already seen a player get accidentally punched in the head by one of these “peanut punches”. I get the feeling that the league will continue to allow this practice despite obvious safety concerns because the punches can result in turnovers and looks good on Sportscenter. I also think it’s basically impossible for the ball carriers to truly secure the ball against these punches. Thoughts?

Ed says: Chris, no, there have not been any statements about the Peanut Punch that I am aware of. The league did fine Dre Greenlaw for striking the helmet of Atlanta Falcons wide receiver on a missed punch. Maybe it comes up during the offseason when new rules are discussed. Until then, I don’t think anything changes.

Darren Silver asks: Supposing JJ McCarthy continues to play well and the Giants make the playoffs as a result, does it really make sense to then trade him for draft picks? Since he’s on a manageable contract, I think having a starting caliber QB back-up is much more valuable than any extra draft picks he might attract. We know Dart (or any starting QB) can go down in a heartbeat. Why not have QB insurance to save us from losing a season due to another Dart injury? I don’t think even a first round pick is as valuable as that would be.

Ed says: Darren, there is a line between having a good backup quarterback and having a full-blown quarterback controversy over who should be the starter. That can divide a locker room, a coaching staff, a fan base, and the media that pumps out content about the team every day. Nobody wants “who is playing quarterback this week?” to be a question that gets asked consistently. Or, for fans to start chanting the backup’s name the first time the starter plays poorly.

If McCarthy plays well enough, that is is the risk you run. If he plays well enough the rest of the season to deserve to be a starting quarterback, you automatically set up a “who’s team is it?” situation if they are both on the 2027 roster. Those never work out well.

Jameis Winston is the quarterback insurance, and he is fine for a few games. A lot of teams would love to have him.

The only way I see McCarthy and Dart both being on the team next season is if McCarthy plays OK, but the overall body of work makes it clear that the ceiling is higher with Dart and there is zero question about who is No. 1.

I still believe the ideal scenario is that McCarthy plays well enough to create a robust market for him this offseason, and that the Giants are able to turn that fifth-round pick they used to acquire him into multiple draft picks of higher value.

Could McCarthy play so well that the Giants actually decide to put Dart on the market in the offseason? Sure. But, we are nowhere close to that yet. It has been five quarters of football.

Tom Donlan asks: What is the biggest roster weakness that you think could prevent the Giants from winning the division, and how realistic can it (they) be upgraded via trade this year, and which parts of the Giants success look sustainable beyond this season so they challenge for the division with regularity? Also, when you look back at this deadline two years from now, what decision – or decision to stand pat – would tell us the Giants evaluated themselves correctly?

Ed says: Tom, I think the biggest roster weakness the Giants need to address is defensive tackle. D.J. Reader is the only good, reliable interior defensive lineman they have. The run defense has been good at times, porous at other times. You can’t consistently defend the run if you can’t consistently hole the line of scrimmage.

The sustainable part of the Giants is that they will have John Harbaugh for the next few years. Rosters change, and there are a lot of unforeseen things. I think we have to see what decisions ultimately get made before speculating on the last part of the question. The generic answer would simply be the tell-tale sign of whether or not the Giants did the right thing would be how much success they have beyond this year.

Ronald Buchheim asks: Ed, have you talked with trainers or doctors about groin injuries in general or the one that Andrew Thomas has? Do you know whether it is wise to play through these injuries rather than resting completely? And whether playing through risks the injury becoming chronic and hampering the player’s subsequent career?

Ed says: Ronald, I have not asked anyone. Players play through injuries all the time. I’m sure there is some risk of making the injury worse, but the Giants wouldn’t put him out there if he wasn’t capable of playing or was risking damaging his career.

Michael Buscemi asks: Trying to understand the Colts philosophy — there’s four or five teams interested in Taylor. I don’t understand at this point the Colts demands if they want a number one and no one stepping up to the plate to pay a number one they have two choices — the first don’t do a trade, keep Taylor.

By playing him this week they risked the factor of injury which removes any trade ability why take a chance if you really want to trade him trade him or do nothing? Again the risk of injury playing him could remove any possible trade.

Ed says: Michael, the Colts, it seems, are going to play this out all the way to the trade deadline on Tuesday and see if anyone will get desperate and up their offer. There is risk, but if they hold him out and then don’t trade him that is not a good look for Indianapolis.

Brennan Lyons asks: I was wondering if you guys have heard any solid rumors about us pursuing Brian Thomas of Jacksonville? I really liked him coming out of LSU, along with Nabers, a few years ago. I would love to see them paired up again on the Giants.

I have seen reports that the Jaguars are looking for depth at Edge and are apparently intent on getting rid of Thomas. Do you think there would be any chance of trading Thibs for him? I doubt we will resign him after this year but I’m not so sure we would be willing to let him go now that we are in the midst of a legitimate playoff run. Do you think we can effectively replace Thibs for the rest of the season?

Long term, we would have control of Thomas for two more years than Thibs. Do you think the Giants would make that move?

Ed says: Brennan, I have not. The Giants, by all accounts, are focused on adding at defensive tackle or taking a big swing at a star running back.

I understand the idea of trading Kayvon Thibodeaux. The issue with that is that the Giants have already lost Brian Burns, Tremaine Edmunds, and Chauncey Golston to injury. Thibodeaux is important to the defense right now. If the Giants were not in prime position to make a playoff run trading Thibodeaux would be an obvious move. Now? Love him or not, he is an important piece of the defense.

Joseph LoBue asks: I found the Compensatory Free Agent chart that you put together last week quite informative (from a CFA process perspective) but even more interesting from a roster-building perspective. In theory, the chart suggests that, on paper, four of the free agents that the Giants gave up (Flott, Bellinger, Belton, Schlottman) were of roughly equivalent value to four that they gained (Likely, Newsome II, Stout, Ricard). In other words, on paper, the league viewed the two sets as equal. However, in reality, the four that they gained (in terms of talent, impact and fit) seem way more valuable from a roster-building standpoint than the four they lost. I recognize that this is a small sample size, but it further suggests to me that Harbaugh really knows what he is doing in getting more for less. Your thoughts?

Ed says: Joseph, I’m glad you found that informative. I don’t know that I would draw any conclusions. Three of the players you mentioned — Isaiah Likely, Jordan Stout, Patrick Ricard — are all players Harbaugh brought with him from Baltimore.

item.title: The 236½-sack nightmare: Aaron Donald, Myles Garrett ready to 'have some fun'
item.description: For the first time this season, Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald will be playing at the same time for the Rams. Will they form an unstoppable pass-rush duo?
item.content:encoded:
It began as something merely conceptual, a tantalizing possibility.

Last June, immediately after the Rams traded for star edge rusher Myles Garrett, the NFL grapevine began buzzing:

Would Aaron Donald, a three-time NFL defensive player of the year, consider coming out of retirement to play with Garrett, a two-time winner of the award?

After a summer of rampant speculation, Donald signed on to join what was already regarded as a Super Bowl-favorite team.

But Donald’s ramp-up to achieve football shape precluded him from playing in the season opener against the San Francisco 49ers. And Garrett underwent knee surgery after that loss, so the two stars were unable to play together for seven games.

On Sunday, it will finally happen.

Barring an unexpected setback, Garrett and Donald will line up together for the first time when the Rams play the Washington Commanders at Northwest Field in Landover, Md.

Two players accustomed to being double- or triple-teamed — two players with a combined 236½ sacks — are eager for opportunities.

“The offenses are really going to have to pick their poison,” said Garrett, who amassed an NFL season-record 23 sacks last season. “‘Who’s going to be freed-up this play?’

“I think either of us are pretty good at winning one-on-ones, so we’ll have some fun.”

Said Donald, one of the most dominant interior linemen in NFL history: “It’s always good when you’ve got all the pieces to the puzzles out there.”

The Rams (4-4) aim to build on their modest two-game winning streak and get over .500 for the first time this season.

The defense will be without cornerback Jaylen Watson, who suffered a season-ending shoulder injury in last Sunday’s victory over the Chargers. Cornerback Trent McDuffie is questionable after suffering a back injury against the Chargers and not practicing this week.

But Garrett’s return should energize a team that still intends to play in Super Bowl LXI at SoFi Stadium.

The Rams have only 12 sacks, which is tied for 26th among 32 teams. Edge rusher Byron Young has a team-best 4½ sacks. Donald is still looking for his first.

The attention the Commanders and future opponents must pay to Garrett and Donald will open play-making opportunities for others, Young said.

“I always call it art,” he said of Garrett’s and Donald’s ability to excel despite double teams. “Because it’s not easy when you’ve got four hands on you 90% of the time. And they still make it work.

“So it’s going to be fun. I can’t wait.”

Defensive lineman Braden Fiske said players are acclimating to Garrett’s skill set and play style.

Read more:Rams vs. Commanders: How to watch, start time, prediction and odds

“I’m sure there will be some kinks to work out early on, but it’s still pretty early in the season,” Fiske said. “He’s been playing for 10 years, so it shouldn’t be too hard to catch his stride.

“But he looks damn good out there.”

Rams left tackle Alaric Jackson played against Garrett in 2023, when the Rams defeated the Cleveland Browns at SoFi Stadium. The 6-foot-4, 272-pound Garrett’s size, speed and burst at the snap is “amazing,” Jackson said.

“He’s like a running back with skill but like a D-lineman with his power,” Jackson said. “He’s good at change of direction — like on a dime...

“He’s kind of like a do-everything kind of guy who’s seen everything as far as looks.”

Coach Sean McVay wants Garrett to “play within himself” Sunday.

Read more:Rams’ Quentin Lake texted apology to Chargers Justin Herbert for ham-handed ‘deli meat’ comment

“He doesn’t have to do anything other than be Myles and play one-eleventh of what the rest were asking to do for the defense,” McVay said.

Garrett said he won’t fight the excitement, the joy and all the emotions of finally getting to play again.

“You don’t try to push them back,” he said. “You open yourself to them. You accept it.

“After acknowledging it, you go out there and do what you’ve always done.”

item.content:encoded:
The Rams’ trip across the country to play the Washington Commanders on Sunday will be a homecoming of sorts for coach Sean McVay, safety Kam Curl and cornerback Emmanuel Forbes Jr.

McVay was a Washington assistant for seven years before the Rams hired him in 2017 and made the then-30-year-old McVay the youngest coach in modern NFL history. McVay was an assistant tight ends coach and tight ends coach under Mike Shanahan and offensive coordinator under Jay Gruden.

“I look back and think of what a pain in the butt I was as an OC, now being in this chair, and how patient [Gruden] was with me and how protected I really felt,” said McVay, who guided the Rams to a road victory over the Commanders in 2020.

Curl played his first four NFL seasons for the Commanders after they selected him in the seventh round of the 2020 draft out of Arkansas. The Commanders did not re-sign him, and he joined the Rams on a two-year contract that included $6 million in guarantees.

Curl made several big plays for the Rams — including last season’s game-clinching interception in the NFL divisional-round victory over the Chicago Bears — and the Rams gave him a three-year extension that includes $24 million in guarantees.

“Had a little bitter breakup, you know, but it is what it is at this point,” Curl said of the Commanders. “I haven’t been back to [the region] since, so it’s going to feel good. Somewhat at home. Emotions will probably be high but keep them in check. ... It’s going to be fun.”

The Commanders selected Forbes with the 16 overall pick in the 2023 draft. He struggled as a rookie and was waived during the next season. The Rams claimed Forbes, and he has regained confidence mostly as a rotational player. With Jaylen Watson out for the season because of a shoulder injury, Josh Wallace and Forbes could see a lot of action.

Forbes said is “a way different player and a way different person” than he was during his time with the Commanders.

“Things happen and it’s in the past,: he said, “but we’ll be ready to go.”

item.title: NFL predictions: Shedeur Sanders vs. Tyler Shough, a battle of last year’s rookie QBs in Browns-Saints
item.description: Can Shedeur Sanders deliver in relief for the Cleveland Browns?
item.content:encoded:
This Sunday, the Cleveland Browns (5-3) take on the New Orleans Saints (2-5). Below, we analyze a few advantages, disadvantages, or general thoughts about the two teams before getting to our predictions for the game.

What Happened to the Confidence?

The news that Shedeur Sanders would suddenly be starting this week, due to the concussion reported by Deshaun Watson, definitely caught us off guard. Due to Watson’s 5-3 record as starter, the boo birds toward him have largely stopped, even though he’s not exactly lighting it up week in and week out. Still, when the news broke, I thought we would see a lot of intrigue from fans regarding Sanders again. Instead, it’s seemed like the opposite. Everyone almost seems resigned to thinking it’ll be a pretty rough game for the second-year quarterback.

I guess I’m a bit caught off guard that the reaction has seemed so tame, or almost like fans are chalking this one up as a loss because of Sanders.

Going back to last year, Sanders did what I would call a respectable job. I thought he showed he can make a lot of good NFL throws, he stopped the bad habit of backpedaling too much, and he did so behind a terrible offensive line. Despite the pace of sacks that this year’s group is giving up, the eye test still tells me that the Browns’ new offensive line is performing way better than last year’s group was. Sanders had some good outings in training camp, and is facing a Saints defense that ranks near the bottom of the league. My expectation is that Sanders will have a solid 2026 debut against New Orleans. This is also a big game, so I’d expect the team to pull out all the stops if necessary.

Assessing the Game

There’s a lot to look at for this week’s game, especially pertaining ti the Browns’ run defense and the Saints’ offense. Let’s get into it with some of our miscellaneous notes this week:

  • I was intrigued by the Saints because last year, they won four straight games near the end of last season, and Tyler Shough was turning headlines and looking like the best quarterback of his class. Now, in hindsight, they didn’t face the best competition in those four games, but it was still something to be proud of.
  • This year, they lost a nailbiter of an overtime opener to the Lions 31-30 when they went for the win in extra time instead of the tie, and then they beat the Baltimore Ravens (back when they had Lamar Jackson) the following week.
  • Since then, it’s been much of the same story: Shough plays well and should be taken seriously, but New Orleans can’t get anything going on the ground, averaging just 3.52 yards per carry. Their numbers and commitment to the ground game has been really bad. I know some of you may be thinking, ‘Welp, get ready for that to change against Cleveland,’ but I’m inclined to expect the opposite: this is a game will New Orleans’ run struggles continue, and the Browns’ run defense feels like they are on top of the world with all the run plays they’ll swallow up.
  • The other thing that has been part of the same story is the Saints’ poor run defense and defensive interior. They allow 4.81 yards per carry, which is well worse than even the Titans’ allowed two weeks ago when the Browns found success on the ground. Comparatively speaking, the Steelers’ run defense is ranked among the best in the league
  • Overall, those factors make me see the Browns having a variety of ways they can score on offense, as long as they stay away from delays and procedural errors (easier said than done, obviously). And while Shough has been pass-heavy, that approach should play into Cleveland’s favor against a duo of Denzel Ward and Tyson Campbell that is playing very well.
  • One big factor to watch is that Saints WR Jordyn Tyson practiced this week for the first time. The first-round pick hasn’t seen regular season action yet, which is crazy. He is listed as questionable, so we’ll see if he is active or inactive.
  • Carson Schwesinger was a liability last week, but that’s a rarity, even if he is hurt. Hopefully we see a bounceback game from him this week.
  • Jared Verse is driving me a bit crazy. Even if I disregard his stats with the Browns, I don’t like the demeanor he carries in interviews, and I feel like he’s the one that has gotten away with some dumb late hits on quarterbacks this year. I’d be rolling my eyes at some of the stuff he says, and if I’m thinking of it, I bet some teammates are keeping a lid on it too. With all that said, I of course want him to flip the switch and be better for the Browns. Not that I’m comparing him to Myles Garrett, but to a much lesser extent, this would be like Garrett going to the Rams and then suddenly looking like a third-string backup with them and unlike his previous years of productivity.
  • According to FanDuel, the Browns are 3 point underdogs against the Saints. The over/under is 43.5.

Quick Hitters

Offensive coordinator Travis Switzer talked about what he’s excited to see from Shedeur Sanders:

“I’m just excited to see him go play and hopefully let it rip, which I think he’ll do. He did it yesterday in practice. Go lead, be in command, which I think he’s grown tremendously in that area, really since we got here. And I think Monk (Todd Monken) mentioned this the other day, but when you’re going through training camp, and we were splitting, and really all the spring, we were splitting a lot of those reps as we were going through all the installs, and we were able to see him in a lot more reps than probably a typical backup would be, because obviously we were finding out who our quarterback was going to be. So, hopefully he can review back to some of those things if it were to be him, and yeah, let it rip. Play with confidence.”

Defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg had some very generic responses to his questions this week, which was a bit disappointing. Ultimately, I’ll highlight this one, when he was asked about the team’s defensive ends not having many combined sacks this year:

“Our whole defense is built on a collective 11, so it has nothing to do with a position ever. We’re not built that way. When it comes to pressuring the quarterback, it doesn’t matter who the pressure could come from. When it comes to anything we do, it’s a collective 11. It takes all 11 to play great defense, and that will always be our motto together.”

Special teams coordinator Bryon Storer was asked about trying different guys out at kick returner lately:

“So, we’re trying some different returners back there. We’ve kind of mixed and matched a little bit over the last couple, last game, and we need to block better in the setup zone. We need to, set up our blocking better. We need to make sure that we stay with our man longer without holding. There’s a lot that goes into it. We’ve been drilling it and trying to get better, and it’s a matchup-based play as well. You know, it’s very much like, you have to make sure you have the right people in the right spots. And so, we’re just continuing to learn and improve each and every week, and hopefully we’ll see some progress there soon.”

Here are predictions from multiple staff members at DBN:

Predictions

Chris Pokorny: “I wanted to pick the Browns by a slightly larger margin, but because the Browns’ victories this year have all been by 3 or 4 points only, and I could foresee some rust from the quarterback spot, I have this as a lower-scoring affair.” Browns 20, Saints 17

Jared Mueller: “Something is off with the Browns and I can’t put my finger on it, but I don’t feel comfortable with it. Injuries, Shedeur Sanders and Jared Verse media time, and going on the road with a team coming off the bye all smell trouble for my favorite team. The Saints are far from a good team but have a creative offensive mind, an athletic quarterback, and enough talent on the roster to win games.” Saints 28, Browns 24

Barry Shuck: “I am on the fence with this one. If you look at the Browns’ schedule, they beat the Ravens and the Steelers, and all of their other wins are against mediocre teams. The only good team they faced, Jacksonville, took Cleveland to the woodshed. And this is their entire schedule because they are involved in that last-place schedule from 2025. The only crappy teams they don’t play are the Dolphins and Cardinals. The Browns can’t stop the run, and they can’t run the ball themselves. Nawlins is ranked #20 in passing yards and #29 in rushing. Which means they can’t run the ball either. They are top half in pass defense, but can’t stop the run either. Whoever wins, it isn’t going to be a very productive day. By the way, M.J. Emerson is the starting CB for the Saints and is doing pretty well. Hold on, let me flip a coin: it’s Cleveland.” Browns 13, Saints 10

Ezweav: “Hard to believe losing Deshaun Watson would make things seem bleak but here we are.  I really like Shedeur Sanders personally (also a big fan of his ‘ol man) but unfortunately his entire professional career to this point can be summed up this way: holds the ball forever, still misses the read.

I know a lot of people have a great deal of hope invested in the kid and I would LOVE for that to be justified but it just hasn’t shown up yet at the NFL level.  Look for folks to start murmuring about Dillon Gabriel by about the middle of the second quarter.” Saints 20, Browns 9

Curtiss Brown: “If Deshaun Watson was starting I would feel somewhat comfortable that the Browns could win but since he’s in concussion protocol, I don’t feel as confident.

I don’t think Shedeur Sanders is a bad quarterback. I just don’t have enough confidence in him looking competent enough and keeping the offense on schedule. I could be wrong though and I look foolish.

The Saints have been a disappointment this season. Quarterback Tyler Shough is doing the most despite not having a run game (Saints firing the run game coordinator doesn’t fix it) their offensive line has been abysmal but the receiver room has something in Chris Olave and Jordyn Tyson will probably make his debut on Sunday if he’s healthy.

Defensively, the Saints haven’t been good. Chase Young has been though. Martin Emerson is making the most on his prove it deal. Overall, this team hasn’t been great and the coaching staff has been under a microscope by the owner and it’s only a matter of time if a head coaching move is made.

Overall, the Browns could win this game but they probably wont (they aren’t favored) but it feels all the positivity around the team evaporated after one bad game and now everyone is on edge again.” Saints 24, Browns 20

item.title: 3-Point Stance: Patriots’ trade deadline isn’t time for a youth movement
item.description: New England shouldn’t rush into midseason roster changes
item.content:encoded:
Are the New England Patriots sellers at the NFL trade deadline?

Last week, Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer highlighted defensive tackle Christian Barmore and cornerback Carlton Davis as potential Patriots trade candidates ahead of the deadline on Tuesday, Nov. 10. According to Breer, if a deal is struck, New England’s motivation would be centered around adding draft capital and transitioning into a younger roster.

Though based on his response when speaking with the media on Wednesday, head coach Mike Vrabel appears to disagree with that approach.

“I think sometimes national reports have the tendency to do that. I have not shared that information with anybody,” Vrabel said. “This time of year, I think that all these things kind of get drummed up. So, we’re focused on trying to prepare for [the Green Bay Packers on Sunday] and make the corrections from [last week].

“This is business as normal here, so I don’t know where a lot of these things come from. Certainly not from any conversations with me.”

Regardless of whether or not the Patriots strike a deal involving either player, trading almost any impact contributor on the roster while sitting at a 5-3 record at the regular season’s midway point is certainly questionable.

At the least, a deal of that stature calls for a corresponding “buying” move.

Sure, New England’s depth in multiple areas will be a largely discussed topic throughout the offseason regarding the team’s roster-building process. And rightfully so.

Vrabel said it himself after a preseason victory over the Philadelphia Eagles, stating at the time that he doesn’t think his team is “very deep.”

But sending away either Barmore or Davis simply doesn’t make sense at this time. Especially for a franchise still in contention for the AFC East title.

Trading Barmore creates another need

In 2023, Barmore posted his best season as a pro, recording 8.5 sacks, 16 quarterback hits and pressuring those passers 49 times. He also consistently disrupted opposing run offenses, forcing 13 tackles for a loss and totaling 64 combined takedowns.

That season-long performance earned the Patriots’ 2021 second-round draft selection a four-year, $84 million contract extension the following offseason.

Currently in year two of that new deal, Barmore’s production hasn’t entirely matched the monetary value of his contract, especially in run defense. From just last season, the 27-year-old has seen his involvement in that facet of the defense drop from 62.8% to just 36%.

Still, New England evidently continues to view Barmore as a producer when rushing the quarterback, heavily using the defensive tackle during pass-rush downs and critical third-down plays.

Barmore’s overall reduced role also doesn’t mean he’s expendable. Trading him shuffles the defensive line, forcing Cory Durden into a new, pass-rush-heavy role and 34-year-old DaQuan Jones, who has contributed as a relief piece for the primary starters, into a heavier workload.

Davis’ departure would leave a hole in the secondary

As for Davis, the cornerback hasn’t shown signs of regression. But the soon-to-be 30-year-old, entering the final year of his contract with a mighty injury history and owed $22 million in 2027, plays directly into the youth-movement argument.

Nonetheless, shipping him off to another franchise creates a glaring hole in the cornerback room. That decision then forces Vrabel and the defensive coaching staff to decide between starting substitute Charles Woods opposite Christian Gonzalez or pulling Marcus Jones away from his natural nickel-cornerback position.

With several offenses in the Patriots’ remaining schedule currently ranking top 10 in passing yards per game, that potential decision seems counterproductive.

Davis, who recently returned to the starting lineup last week after missing four games, played a significant role in New England’s divisional round victory against the Houston Texans in the playoffs last season, intercepting C.J. Stroud twice.

The offseason offers a better time to make a move

It’s true that the Patriots’ defense has struggled to deliver on the expectations surrounding their offseason additions of Dre’Mont Jones, All-Pro safety Kevin Byard and second-round pick Gabe Jacas. But much like the rest of the roster, that group has dealt with injuries.

Last week’s matchup against the Miami Dolphins marked the first game the starting cornerback trio of Gonzalez, Davis and Jones all played together since Week Three.

While the healthy defense didn’t put together a flawless performance, the unit signaled improvement, sacking Malik Willis on five occasions, logging an interception and forcing the Miami offense into four three-and-out possessions.

Teams can afford slow starts, and while there’s no guarantee New England will find its stride later in the season, the ability to play its best football down the stretch is what ultimately matters the most.

In Barmore’s case, as the Boston Herald’s Andrew Callahan put it, the Patriots seemingly want “out of the Barmore business.”

An offseason deal, rather than a midseason trade, allows New England greater flexibility to reallocate resources and explore replacements to replicate or improve upon Barmore’s production while spending less.

Even though eventually moving Barmore or another established contributor makes sense for the team’s long-term roster construction, the Patriots’ timing of a potential trade should account for the franchise’s current position in the AFC playoff picture.

item.title: Chargers vs. Texans: How to watch, start time, prediction and odds
item.description: Everything you need to know about the Chargers facing the Houston Texans on Sunday, including how to watch, betting odds, injuries and a score prediction.
item.content:encoded:
Heading into the season, the Chargers might have circled Sunday’s game against Houston on their calendar. This was the chance to take down the Texans, who knocked them out of the playoffs in 2024 then beat them again last season.

The conversation is markedly different now.

It’s Week 9, maybe the Chargers can finally win a game.

Read more:Rams’ Quentin Lake texted apology to Chargers Justin Herbert for ham-handed ‘deli meat’ comment

They are 5½-point underdogs at home, and for good reason. Not only are the Chargers the NFL’s only winless team, but they have gone 27 consecutive drives without a touchdown, and quarterback Justin Herbert leads the league with 10 interceptions.

It has been a forehead-slapping tumble for a team some people predicted might wind up in the Super Bowl, which will be played at SoFi Stadium. The Chargers won 11 games in back-to-back seasons. Now, they have the inside track on the No. 1 overall pick.

All that makes Houston’s sluggish start almost quaint by comparison. The Texans are 2-5, and their defense, long the strength of their team, is ranked a ho-hum 19th in yards allowed.

The Texans were off last week, and before that won two of their three previous games, road wins over Tennessee and Jacksonville.

If there’s any remaining buzz surrounding the Chargers, it’s what should they do at offensive coordinator. Mike McDaniel has been a fiasco in his first season, and Herbert looks out of sync and even lost. The coordinator plans to move from the sideline up into the booth for this game, hoping that will give him a better play-calling vantage.

Hard to imagine it getting worse.

Key injuries

Texans: RB David Montgomery (groin, out); S Reed Blankenship (concussion/hand, out).

Chargers: CB Deane Leonard (concussion, out); S Kendall Williamson (calf, out); WR Brenen Thompson (quad/hamstring, questionable); TE David Njoku (fibula, questionable); G Kayode Awosika (fibula, questionable); LB Denzel Perryman (pectoral, questionable).

The Chargers and Houston Texans will play Sunday at 1:05 p.m. PST at SoFi Stadium. The game will be shown in Southern California on CBS and Paramount+. It will be available nationally via a subscription to NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube TV. In Southern California, fans can listen to the game on 640 AM and 103.9 FM.

Sam Farmer’s pick: The law of averages says the Chargers are going to win a game at some point, and their defense has played well for long stretches. But until their offense gets some semblance of traction, it’s hard to pick them. Texans 23, Chargers 13

item.title: Cowboys news: Jerry Jones tries to walk back ‘paying coaches’ comments
item.description: Here is today's Dallas Cowboys news.
item.content:encoded:
Jerry Jones has been criticized for not being willing to write a huge check for a championship type of coach, but he doesn’t feel that it’s an issue whatsoever.

The NFL trade deadline is rapidly approaching. If Dallas was to indulge, there’s one area that’s likely to get the most attention. The Cowboys have a talented offense that more than capable of being productive, but hiccups at the wrong times have caused some confusion.

Cowboys’ Jerry Jones says paying coaches has never been an issue – Todd Archer, ESPN

Jerry Jones got ridiculed after he mentioned that there was no connection between the highest-paid coaches to winning championships. Now, he’s saying spend top dollar for a coach hasn’t been a problem in Dallas.

“The facts are I have been out there, and I have been trying to lure very successful coaches away from the teams they were on and knew full well that I was going to pay them for their success,” he said. “So that has been done. No one knows that, but I do. And so it is absolutely ridiculous. And I actually grin when somebody says, ‘Jerry’s not willing to pay the money for what it would take to get the right kind of coach out there.'”

Cowboys to be without two starters, four more questionable vs. Colts – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram

The Cowboys are facing a huge game against the Colts as they try to stay within striking distance in the NFC East. They’ll have to do so with multiple starters out.

On Friday, the Cowboys hit the practice field for the last time before boarding the flight to Indianapolis on Saturday, and they did so without two starters. Wide receiver and kick returner KaVontae Turpin (ribs) and rookie outside linebacker Malachi Lawrence (ankle) did not practice this week and have been ruled out for Sunday’s game.

Which position group could Cowboys add to at trade deadline? Stephen Jones answers – SportsDay Staff, Dallas Morning News

The NFL deadline is next Tuesday, and the Cowboys have been talked about as a team that could make a move. The specific position that they could make a play for was revealed.

Q: Which position or positions do you think could help the team the most right now?

Jones: “Yeah I think it’s one everybody talks [about], obviously a pressure player could help us. After that, we took care of business earlier in the year with [Joey Porter Jr.]. It’s unfortunate he’s been missing some time. No excuses, because everybody has injuries, but no question it hurt us not having him or Caleb [Downs] in the game there in that quarter as well.”

item.title: Reacts Results: Settling expectations into the gutter
item.description: The Panthers are down, but not out. How much further they slide depends a lot on what they can pull together against the Broncos
item.content:encoded:
Go back into the comments this week on almost any article and you’ll find a number of our readers referencing “shuffling the deck chairs on the titanic.” That’s the mood across the Carolina Panthers fandom after two consecutive, demoralizing losses that have highlighted both the weaknesses of the coaching staff and the limitations of this heavily injured roster.

Fan confidence, which was riding in the 90s for a couple of week as the Panthers built themselves up to a 3-2 record after their early bye week, has cratered. The inability of the remains of Carolina’s offensive line to do anything with much success has hamstrung the high-flying offense that began the season with hopes of an NFL-leading passer and whispers of the MVP conversation. Now, instead of an award, the team views a first down as a lofty aspiration.

Staff firings aren’t surprising with these kinds of confidence numbers. Many have been out on Evero for years as his “bend but don’t break” style of defense too often broke. What is telling, however, is that most Panthers fans don’t think his removal moves the needle much. Head coach Dave Canales has a battle ahead of him to not lose the fanbase entirely. From one perspective, it is simple: start winning again. From another, it is much harder.

Just as fans are right not to expect major changes for a unit devastated by injury just because their much-maligned leader has been fired, fans also shouldn’t expect a massive change in the Panthers ability to compete. They are fielding what is, at many positions, a roster with less reliable or less heralded players than they had during the preseason. Cornerback and left guard have been particularly affected. Left tackle, center, and right guard have experienced much less turmoil and yet also been somehow more disappointing as the season has worn on.

Some of that blame is rightly laid at Canales’ feet. Coaching plays a part in every players performance and the buck stops with him on that front. Some if it, however, comes down to luck and the players. Injuries, regressions, and mistakes are things that happen. It takes a team effort to overcome them and, for the moment, that effort seems lacking across the board.

There is a fear among fans and media members about the power of “bulletin-board material.”

According to the theory, if a player or coach says something negative (either real or perceived) about the upcoming team on the schedule, that quote will be printed out and posted on a bulletin board for everyone on the opposing team to see.

It is a bit of an antiquated idea – has anyone actually used a bulletin board since the last millennium? – but it was probably always more about the message than the medium anyway.

The real question is just how much does that actually happen across professional sports? These are highly skilled athletes making a good living and eager to keep it that way. Do they really need to be motivated by something another player may (or may not) have said in the build-up to the game?

Well, we’re going to find out come Sunday when the Cleveland Browns take on the New Orleans Saints, as defensive end Carl Granderson is a bit out of joint over comments from Cleveland quarterback Shedeur Sanders.

“We have a chip on our shoulde for sure. They’ve been chirping a little bit. We see what the quarterback done said. So we going to come in hot and ready to play. It’s going to be a good game for sure.

One would think the Saints would be “hot and ready to play” even without some pretty tame comments from a player who is going to make one start before heading back to the bench. But to each their own.

item.title: 3 overlooked Joe Burrow throws that helped Bengals defeat Titans
item.description: Joe Burrow is spreading the ball around to a deep group of pass-catchers.
item.content:encoded:
Seven players caught at least one pass from Joe Burrow in Sunday’s 43-36 overtime win for the Bengals over the Tennessee Titans. Samaje Perine and Jack Endries were both only targeted one time.

Perine hauled in a nine-yard reception on the second play of overtime, and Endries hauled in a one-yard touchdown that gave the Bengals a 14-13 lead just before halftime.

Coming into this season, there was a lot of conversation about the Bengals’ wide receiver depth behind Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. Sunday, though, showed that depth is good heading into mid-November. Mike Gesicki has a touchdown in five straight games and six out of seven overall this season, and Dohnte Meyers has gone from a great training camp story to an integral part of the Bengals’ receiver room and special teams.

Burrow has trust in a lot of receivers right now. Several players caught passes from Burrow in the fourth quarter and overtime Sunday in got-to-have-it situations.

On a day where Burrow was historically good, three throws are getting overlooked, but they stand out for the growing trust he has in the Bengals deep group of pass catchers and also for how ridiculously accurate and prolific Joe Burrow is at throwing the football.

1. 10:07 4Q — 3rd&3 from the Bengals 34-yard line; Bengals trailing 28-23

Tensions were high in Paycor Stadium going into this play. The Bengals had just turned the ball over on their previous offensive possession, their fourth of the day, and Tennessee cashed in with a touchdown to take the lead. After a Chase Brown run on 2nd&4 gained just one yard, there were boo-birds coming down from the crowd. Then on 3rd&3, Burrow coolly found Mike Gesicki on the right side of the field for 18 yards and a badly needed first down.

It was just Gesicki’s second catch of the game, but it would be the first of three receptions for him in the fourth quarter that accumulated 48 yards. Four plays after his third-down reception, Gesicki hauled in a 25-yard touchdown for his sixth score of the season and to give the Bengals a 29-28 lead. Gesicki is now tied for the most touchdowns he’s ever scored in a season, and that was back in 2020, when he caught six touchdowns in his third season with the Dolphins.

This season, Gesicki has 17 receptions for 241 yards and six touchdowns, averaging 14.2 yards per reception.

Fourteen of Gesicki’s 17 receptions are for first downs or touchdowns. He set the tone for this season in Week 1, catching five passes for 78 yards and a touchdown, including three catches for 52 yards on the Bengals’ final first-half drive that led to a field goal. Now, Gesicki has a touchdown in five straight games, the longest streak for a tight end in Bengals’ franchise history.

2. 8:03 4Q — 3rd&10 from the Titans’ 48-yard line; Bengals trailing 28-23

Don’t let Gesicki’s emergence and Tee’s career-year overshadow the incredible connection Burrow and Chase have. They’ve been on the same page going all the way back to their first season at LSU in 2018. This play on Sunday shows the timing Burrow and Chase have on a difficult throw as Burrow is getting hit from a defensive stunt.

First of all, this play was set up by a 10-yard reception by Chase Brown on 2nd&20, which the Bengals were in after Burrow was sacked on first down. So getting back into third-and-manageable is impressive in and of itself.

Then on 3rd&10, the Titans ran a stunt with defensive end Jacob Martin looping around the left side of the Bengals’ offensive line. It gave him a free rush at Burrow, but he didn’t sack him. While he hit him hard, Burrow got rid of the ball just in time and layered a throw around multiple Titans’ defenders to Chase on the far side of the field.

It gained 23 yards, and it set up Gesicki’s 25-yard touchdown on the next play.

Chase had 11 receptions for 141 yards and a touchdown on Sunday, his first game with 100+ receiving yards and his first game with 10+ receptions. Even though Chase “only” has 492 receiving yards through seven games, he still has six touchdowns on the season, touchdowns in three straight games and five of his last six.

And if Chase has 10 receptions on Sunday, he’ll tie Michael Thomas for the most games with 10+ receptions by a player in his first six seasons all-time with 18.

For what it’s worth, Chase is still on pace for 148 targets, 104 receptions, 1,195 receiving yards, and 15 touchdowns this season. Even if that’s a “down” year, it’d still be a great year. But don’t worry; Chase had eight receptions for 130 yards and two touchdowns the last time the Bengals played the Falcons… and he didn’t even play in the second half of that game.

3. 3:01 4Q — 2nd&3 from the Bengals’ 26-yard line; Bengals trailing 36-29

This is my favorite play of the game. Tennessee just scored what could have been a back-breaking touchdown to take a 36-29 lead. I don’t know about you, but I didn’t know what the Bengals were going to do on their ensuing drive. It felt to me that it could go either way. But after this play, I was confident the Bengals were going to score and tie the game.

Burrow was in trouble on this play, but he bounced out of the pocket and started rolling to his left. It wasn’t Chase or Higgins who caught the pass, though. It was Dohnte Meyers. The standout in training camp and the preseason, and who recently starred in the CFL, came across the field and made a diving 18-yard reception to move the chains and get the offense rolling.

In that big of a spot, with Burrow escaping the pocket, it was Meyers making an incredible catch to gain the Bengals’ first down on the drive that ultimately tied the game late in the fourth quarter.

Five plays later, Tee Higgins caught his second touchdown to tie the game at 36-36.

Through seven games, Meyers has 16 receptions for 175 yards. Ten of those catches are for first downs, and he also has one rush for 10 yards that gained a first down against Tampa Bay. On special teams, Meyers has 11 punt returns for 103 yards and a 9.4 average, and he has 25 kick returns for 660 yards and a 26.4 average. Meyers had three receptions for 34 yards on Sunday, including two receptions in the fourth quarter for 27 yards.

Joe Burrow is averaging 302.1 passing yards per game. Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins both lead the Bengals with 43 receptions. But other players are also stepping up, as evidenced by their performances on Sunday and through seven games this season. The Bengals not only have the best wide receiver duo in the NFL, but they also have one of the NFL’s overlooked but deepest groups of pass catchers.

That may be what lifts Joe Burrow to the pole position of the MVP race and ultimately wins him his first MVP award.

item.title: Giants news: Cam Skattebo doubtful for Sunday, Eagles matchups, more
item.description: New York Giants headlines for Saturday
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the first place Giants get ready to face off tomorrow against the Philadelphia Eagles.

New York Giants’ playoff fate will be heavily influenced by Eagles game | USAToday.com

Based on the analytics and percentages, a Giants win would put them in prime position for a playoff spot. A loss would drop them back deep into the pack. A Giants win would give them a 68 percent chance to win the NFC East and a 71 percent shot at making the playoffs.

A loss would lessen their division odds to 41 percent and their postseason odds to 43 percent. So, this is kind of a “must-win” for Big Blue (4-2-1) as their schedule gets dicey in the second half of the season.

Coach Harbaugh breaking down Texans film

Harbs Weekly: Earn the right to play in memorable games | Giants.com

Q: Getting into November football, is there a new skill that your team has to unlock?

Harbaugh: Everything is new. Every step of the way is going to be new this year. I think it’s kind of what first years are a lot of times. Like we told them, this is November football. You’ve earned the right to play meaningful games in November. What does that mean? What are you playing for? I asked them, “What do they say about December football? Have you heard the old saying?” And someone got it. [Fullback Patrick] Ricard got it. “They remember what you do in December.” That’s right. I said that’s what they remember. I said they won’t really remember November too much. But without November you can’t get to the point where you’re playing games that are going to be memorable. That’s what we’re playing for right now. We’re playing for the opportunity to play in memorable games, and that’s why November is so important and we’ve earned the right to be to be playing in these games. So, it’s just another notch up of value and then I just talked to them a little bit about as the season goes along, it’s still one game but each game becomes worth more. It’s one game, that’s what this is about, but each game becomes even more valuable because there’s more payoff. Later, that’s why they remember what you do in December. There’s more payoff. So, that’s kind of cool.

Giants not looking past Saquon Barkley and struggling Eagles | New York Post

“Before Lane Johnson had a name, before Jason Kelce had a name, before Cam Jurgens had a name, they had to go earn it,” defensive tackle Shelby Harris said. “You can’t put down anybody just because they haven’t established themselves in the league. The idea is you don’t want them to establish themselves against you. They’re still physical, they’re humungous size-wise across the board, so it’s just go out there and don’t let them be the determining factor of the game.”

“I’m expecting [Barkley] to be healthier than he has been so far,” Harris said. “They’ve done a good job trying to manage him on his way back from injury. If he’s going to play, I expect to get the best out of him — full-on star Saquon Barkley. And we’ll have to stop him in order to be successful.”

NFL Week 9 preview: Picks, predictions, schedule, betting odds, fantasy tips | ESPN.com

What we’re hearing on the Giants: The Giants believe the bye week should’ve helped QB J.J. McCarthy. He’s now fully caught up after being traded to New York in late September. McCarthy, who is making his second start for the Giants, expects Eagles DC Vic Fangio to make him “earn it.” It will be the latest test of whether the young QB can succeed while facing simulated pressures and getting through his progressions.

How Skatt and the Giants are fed

Ravens’ Derrick Henry is frustrated. Will Giants’ John Harbaugh try to trade for him? | NJ.com

“I mean, we’ve lost four times [in a row],” Henry said. “It’s frustrating. I don’t have the magical answer. We’ve got to go back to work.” When asked about a potential trade, Henry said, “I have not mentioned me going anywhere else. I’m saying let’s go back to work.”

Henry turns 33 in January. He is under contract through next season. Harbaugh doesn’t want a one-year rental, and Henry technically would not be that. His salary next year is $11 million — all of which is non-guaranteed. He has a $1 million roster bonus due in March. So the Ravens (or Giants) have a team option on him for 2027.

The 10 best NFL player matchups to watch in Week 9 | PFF

New York Giants WR Malik Nabers vs. Philadelphia Eagles CB Quinyon Mitchell. The Giants seek to widen their NFC East lead when they face the Eagles, losers of six in a row. While a battle of backup quarterbacks may be the top storyline, Nabers vs. Mitchell will be must-see television. Nabers has returned from his torn ACL with a vengeance. He’s earned an 82.8 PFF receiving grade with 2.54 yards per route run, numbers that have culminated despite a slower first three games. On top of that, the former sixth overall pick has dropped only two catchable targets all year.

Philadelphia’s defense has regressed in 2026, but not because of Mitchell. He’s generated a 67.2 PFF coverage grade, letting up a 69.2 passer rating into his coverage while enabling just a 54.3% opponent completion percentage. Mitchell has had the advantage when these former 2024 first-round picks have squared off. Across 11 prior matchups, Nabers has gained just one catch for nine yards on two targets, being charted as open only three times.

Giants look to snap losing streak in Philadelphia. If not now, when? | The Athletic

The Giants have had heartbreakers at Lincoln Financial Field, but a loss Sunday would be the worst of the streak because they’re the better team with a far more promising outlook. The Giants are 3.5-point favorites Sunday and winning in Philadelphia would be another step in Harbaugh’s process of rebuilding the franchise.

Harbaugh’s track record suggests the Giants are in a strong position to end the streak. His Ravens teams went 15-3 after the bye during his 18 seasons in Baltimore. “We’ve got everything to gain and we know how big this game is,” Harbaugh said. “We know who we’re going against. We’ll be ready.”

item.title: Myles Garrett: Rams' opponents will have to pick their poison, me or Aaron Donald
item.description: Garrett and Donald will play together for the first time on Sunday against the Commanders.
item.content:encoded:
Rams defensive end Myles Garret and defensive tackle Aaron Donald will finally be on the field together Sunday in Washington, and Garrett says that's going to be bad news for opposing offenses for the rest of the season.

Donald did not play in Week 1 because he was still ramping up for the season after returning from his two-year retirement, and Garret hasn't played since Week 1 because of knee surgery. Garrett said the two of them together, two multiple-time Defensive Player of the Year award winners side by side, will present a unique challenge for opposing offenses.

"I think offenses really have to pick their poison. Who's going to be freed up this play? I think either of us are pretty good at winning one-on-one, so we'll have some fun," Garrett said. "Going into this season I never thought I'd have the chance, and as you all know he kept us in suspense for quite a while, so it was very exciting, and I'm looking forward to getting on the field and playing some real snaps with him."

Garrett said his poor performance in Week 1 against the 49ers showed him he needed knee surgery, something he would have preferred to avoid.

"I was frustrated after the game. I knew that wasn't me, and I was being hampered by something," Garrett said. "I didn't want to miss any time, but I had to be realistic about where I was physically, and I had to make the best choice for me and the team."

But now Garrett is back, and he said he and Donald playing together can give the Rams an "elite defense" for the rest of the season.
